lessons.title: Page structure and semantic tags
lessons.goal: Write a valid HTML5 page and pick tags by meaning, not looks.
body: HTML describes **what** each part of a page is. The browser turns your HTML into a tree of elements called the **DOM**, which CSS styles and JavaScript changes.
Every page starts with `<!DOCTYPE html>`, then `<html>` holding a `<head>` (information about the page) and a `<body>` (what people see).

**Semantic tags** say what content means: `<header>`, `<nav>`, `<main>`, `<article>`, `<footer>`. Screen readers, search engines and other developers all rely on them. A page built only from `<div>`s looks the same but tells nobody anything.

example.code:
Jordan's Bakery

Menu

Menu

Fresh bread every morning.

© 2026 Jordan's Bakery

demo.say: The doctype tells the browser to use modern HTML5 rules.
`lang="en"` tells screen readers and translators the page language.
The head holds information about the page: the character set, mobile scaling, and the title shown in the browser tab.
`<header>` holds the site name and `<nav>` holds the main links.
`<main>` is the unique content of this page. There should be only one per page.
`<footer>` closes the page with small print.

check.q: Which element should wrap the unique content of a page?
check.why: `<main>` marks the page's main content, and there should be one per page.

check.q: Where does the <title> go?
check.why: The title is information about the page, so it lives in `<head>`.

lessons.title: Headings, links, images and lists
lessons.goal: Use the everyday content tags correctly, including alt text.
body: Headings go from `<h1>` to `<h6>`. Use one `<h1>` per page and don't skip levels: an `<h3>` belongs under an `<h2>`.
`<a href="...">` makes a link. **Links go places; buttons do things.** If clicking it doesn't take you to a new URL, it should be a `<button>`.
`` needs an `alt` that says what the image shows. If the image is decoration only, use an empty `alt=""` so screen readers skip it.
`<ul>` is a bulleted list, `<ol>` a numbered list, and each item is an `<li>`.

example.code:
Our Breads

  • Sourdough
  • Rye

How to order

  1. Pick your bread
  2. Call the shop
Full menu

demo.say: An `<h2>` starts a section under the page's `<h1>`.
The alt text describes the image for people who can't see it.
Order doesn't matter in this list, so it's a `<ul>`.
`<h3>` is a sub-section of Our Breads.
Steps happen in order, so they use a numbered `<ol>`.
`target="_blank"` opens a new tab, and `rel="noopener"` stops the new page from controlling yours.

practice.task: Add a Hobbies section to your profile: an `<h2>`, an image with good alt text, and a list of three hobbies.
practice.hint: Is the order of your hobbies important? That decides `<ul>` or `<ol>`.

solution.code:
Hobbies

  • Cycling
  • Cooking
  • Chess

check.q: A clickable element opens a menu without changing the URL. Which tag?
check.why: It performs an action rather than navigating, so it's a button.

check.q: What alt should a purely decorative swirl image have?
check.why: An empty alt tells screen readers to skip it. Leaving alt out makes them read the file name.

lessons.title: Forms and labels
lessons.goal: Build a form where every input has a label and basic validation.
body: A `<form>` groups inputs. Each `<input>` needs a `<label>` connected by matching `for` and `id`. Clicking the label then focuses the input, and screen readers read the label aloud.
The input `type` gives you free behavior: `type="email"` checks for an @, `type="number"` shows a number pad on phones.
`required`, `minlength` and `maxlength` make the browser check the form before it submits. That's **validation** without JavaScript.
Every input needs a `name`. That's the key its value is sent under.

example.code:
<form action="/signup" method="post">
  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email" required>

  <label for="pw">Password</label>
  <input id="pw" name="password" type="password" minlength="8" required>

  <label>
    <input name="news" type="checkbox"> Send me the newsletter
  </label>

  <button type="submit">Sign up</button>
</form>

demo.say: `action` is where the data goes and `method` is how it's sent.
`for="email"` matches `id="email"`, which connects the label to the input.
`minlength="8"` and `required` block submitting until the password is long enough.
Wrapping the input inside the label also connects them, with no `for` needed.
`type="submit"` sends the form. The browser runs its validation first.

practice.task: Build a contact form with name (required), email (required, type email), and message (a `<textarea>`, max 500 characters).
practice.hint: `<textarea>` uses `maxlength` too, and it needs a label like any other input.

solution.code:
<form>
  <label for="name">Name</label>
  <input id="name" name="name" required>
  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email" required>
  <label for="msg">Message</label>
  <textarea id="msg" name="message" maxlength="500"></textarea>
  <button type="submit">Send</button>
</form>

check.q: What connects a <label> to an <input>?
options: for on the label matching id on the input
Putting them next to each other
check.why: `for`/`id` (or nesting the input in the label) makes the connection.

check.q: Which attribute is the key the value is submitted under?
check.why: The form sends `name=value` pairs.

intermediateLessons.title: Accessible forms: groups, hints and errors
intermediateLessons.goal: Group related inputs and connect hints and error messages to the right field.
body: Radio buttons and checkboxes that answer one question belong in a `<fieldset>` with a `<legend>`. Screen readers read the legend before each option, so "Small" becomes "Size: Small".
Connect hint text to its input with `aria-describedby="hint-id"`. It's read after the label.
When a field is wrong, set `aria-invalid="true"` and point `aria-describedby` at the error message too. Put the error **next to the field**, in words, not only in red.
Use `autocomplete` values (`email`, `new-password`, `postal-code`) so browsers and password managers can fill the form.

example.code:
Pizza size

We deliver within 5 miles.

Enter a 5-digit postcode, like 30301.

demo.say: `novalidate` turns off the browser's pop-ups so you can show your own messages.
The fieldset groups the radios, and the legend names the group.
`autocomplete` lets the browser fill it. `aria-describedby` lists two ids: the hint and the error.
`aria-invalid="true"` tells screen readers the value is wrong.
The hint and error are read after the label. The error says how to fix the problem.

check.q: What reads a group's name before each radio option?
check.why: The legend is announced as the group label.

check.q: How do you tie an error message to an input?
options: aria-describedby pointing at the message's id
check.why: aria-describedby links extra text to the field.

intermediateLessons.title: Responsive images, video and captions
intermediateLessons.goal: Serve the right image size for each screen, and caption your videos.
body: `srcset` lists the same image at several widths, and `sizes` tells the browser how wide the image will be shown. The browser then downloads the smallest file that looks sharp.
`` with `` offers modern formats, with the `` as the fallback.
Always set `width` and `height` on images. The browser reserves the space, so the page doesn't jump when the image loads (that jump is called layout shift).
`loading="lazy"` waits to load images until they're near the screen. **Don't** lazy-load the main image at the top of the page.
Videos need captions: a `<track kind="captions">` pointing at a `.vtt` file.

demo.say: Browsers that support AVIF (a smaller format) use this source.
Everyone else gets JPEG, at 400px or 800px wide.
Half the screen on tablets and up, the full width on phones. The browser does the maths.
width and height reserve space, and alt describes the image.
Below the fold, so load it lazily.
A video with controls, a poster frame, and English captions on by default.

intermediateLessons.title: Metadata for search and sharing, plus <details>
intermediateLessons.goal: Write head tags for search results and link previews, and use native disclosure widgets.
body: Every page needs its own `<title>` (about 50–60 characters) and `<meta name="description">` (about 150 characters). Search results show them.
**Open Graph** tags (`og:title`, `og:description`, `og:image`) control the preview card when someone shares your link. Share images are usually 1200×630.
`<link rel="canonical">` tells search engines the main URL when the same page is reachable at several addresses.
`<details>` and `<summary>` make a show/hide section with keyboard support and no JavaScript. They're good for FAQs.

example.code:
Do I need to bring anything?

Just an apron. We supply flour, bowls and a starter jar.

demo.say: Specific, with the most important words first.
Written for people reading search results: what you get and why.
The one true URL for this page.
What a shared link shows. Image URLs must be absolute (start with https).
A collapsible answer. Clicking or pressing Enter on the summary toggles it.

check.q: What controls a link's preview card on social apps?
check.why: og: tags define the title, description and image.

check.q: <details> needs JavaScript to open and close.
check.why: It's built into the browser, keyboard support included.

advancedLessons.title: ARIA patterns, and when not to use ARIA
advancedLessons.goal: Know the first rule of ARIA, and build a disclosure and a live region correctly.
body: **The first rule of ARIA: don't use it if a native element does the job.** A `<button>` is focusable, clickable with Enter and Space, and announced as a button. A `<div role="button">` needs all of that added by hand.
ARIA only changes what assistive technology **hears**. It adds no behavior: `role="button"` doesn't make Enter work.
**States** must stay in sync with what's on screen: `aria-expanded` on a toggle, `aria-pressed` on a toggle button, `aria-current="page"` on the current nav link.

**Live regions** (`aria-live="polite"` or `role="status"`) announce changes that happen without focus moving, like "3 results" or "Saved". The region must exist on the page **before** the text changes.
Test with a real screen reader (VoiceOver on Mac: Cmd+F5; NVDA on Windows), not just automated checkers.

example.code: Two to four business days.

demo.say: A real button (keyboard support for free), plus aria-expanded and aria-controls describing what it opens.
`hidden` removes the panel for everyone, screen readers included.
An empty status region that's already on the page, waiting for messages.
Toggle the panel AND keep aria-expanded in sync. A stale state is worse than none.
Changing the text in the live region makes screen readers announce it without moving focus.

practice.task:
Fix this: `
Save
`.
practice.hint: Rule one of ARIA.

solution.code:
<button type="button" class="btn" onclick="save()">Save</button>
<!-- Not <div role="button" tabindex="0">: you'd also have to handle Enter and Space yourself. -->

check.q: Does role="button" make a div respond to the Enter key?
check.why: ARIA changes semantics only. Use <button>.

check.q: When must a live region exist?
check.why: Screen readers watch regions that are already on the page.

advancedLessons.title: Web Components and <template>
advancedLessons.goal: Build a reusable custom element that works in any framework, or none.
body: **Custom elements** are your own HTML tags, built into the browser: `class Rating extends HTMLElement`, registered with `customElements.define("star-rating", Rating)`. Names must contain a hyphen.
**Shadow DOM** (`this.attachShadow({ mode: "open" })`) gives the component its own private DOM and CSS. Page styles don't leak in, and its styles don't leak out.
`<template>` holds markup that isn't rendered until you clone it, which is ideal for a component's internals.
React, Vue and plain HTML can all use the same web component. Design systems at large companies often ship this way.
Lifecycle: `connectedCallback` (added to the page), `disconnectedCallback` (removed), and `attributeChangedCallback` for the attributes listed in `static observedAttributes`.

example.code: Paid Overdue

demo.say: The template isn't rendered. It's a blueprint to clone.
Styles inside the shadow DOM. `:host([tone=...])` styles the element based on its own attribute.
`<slot>` shows whatever text sits between the tags.
Use it like any HTML tag.
On connect, attach a shadow root and clone the template into it (only once).
Register the tag name. It must contain a hyphen.

practice.task: Make the badge react when its `tone` attribute changes after it's on the page.
practice.hint: `static observedAttributes = ["tone"]` plus `attributeChangedCallback`. With :host styles, CSS already reacts, so try logging the change to see it fire.

check.q: What does Shadow DOM give a component?
options: Private markup and CSS that don't leak in or out
check.why: Encapsulation is the point.

check.q: A valid custom element name is…
check.why: It must be lowercase and contain a hyphen.

advancedLessons.title: Loading performance and structured data
advancedLessons.goal: Load the most important things first, and describe your page to search engines.
body: **Core Web Vitals** are Google's user-experience scores: **LCP** (how fast the main content shows, aim for under 2.5s), **INP** (how fast the page responds to input, under 200ms), and **CLS** (how much the layout jumps, under 0.1).
Help LCP: `fetchpriority="high"` on the hero image, `<link rel="preload">` for a critical font, and never lazy-load what's on screen at the start.
`<script defer>` downloads in parallel and runs after the HTML is parsed. `async` runs as soon as it arrives. Plain `<script>` in the head blocks the page.
**Structured data** (JSON-LD) describes your content in a form search engines read, which can unlock rich results like star ratings, event dates or course listings.

demo.say: Fetch the main font early, so text doesn't swap fonts late.
Open the connection to the image CDN before it's needed.
defer: download now, run after parsing. The page isn't blocked.
JSON-LD tells search engines this page is a Course, and who provides it.
The LCP image: high priority and never lazy.
Below the fold: lazy, and decoded off the main thread.

practice.task: Run Lighthouse (Chrome DevTools → Lighthouse) on your portfolio. Write down LCP, CLS and the top 3 suggestions, then fix one.
practice.hint: Use an incognito window so extensions don't skew the results.

- Add width and height to images (CLS)
- Remove loading="lazy" from the hero and add fetchpriority="high" (LCP)
- Serve AVIF/WebP and correctly sized images (LCP)
- Defer non-critical scripts (LCP/INP)

lessons.title: Selectors and the cascade
lessons.goal: Target elements with selectors and predict which rule wins.
body: A CSS rule is a **selector** plus **declarations**: `p { color: red; }`.
Common selectors: a tag (`p`), a class (`.card`), an id (`#hero`), a descendant (`nav a`), and states (`a:hover`).
When two rules set the same property, **specificity** decides: an id beats a class, a class beats a tag. If they tie, the rule written **later** wins. That's the cascade.
Prefer classes for styling. They're reusable and keep specificity low, so you rarely have to fight your own CSS.

demo.say: Every paragraph turns gray, the lowest specificity.
A paragraph with `class="intro"` turns navy, because a class beats a tag.
`id="special"` beats both: crimson.
Links inside `<nav>` lose the underline, then get it back on hover.
Same selector twice, so the later one wins: the button is gold.

A

matches p, .note and #x rules. Which color wins?
check.why: Id specificity is highest.

check.q: Two rules have equal specificity. Which wins?
check.why: On a tie, source order decides and the later rule wins.

lessons.title: The box model
lessons.goal: Control size and spacing with content, padding, border and margin.
body: Every element is a box with four layers: **content**, then **padding** (space inside the border), then **border**, then **margin** (space outside).

By default `width` sets only the content, so padding and border make the box wider than you asked for. `box-sizing: border-box` makes `width` include padding and border, which is far easier to reason about.
Margins push neighbours away. Padding gives breathing room inside a colored box.

demo.say: Apply border-box to everything. Most projects start with this line.
The card is exactly 300px wide, including padding and border.
16px of space between the border and the text inside.
A 2px sky-blue border.
24px above and below, and `auto` left and right centers the box.

practice.task: Create a `.badge` that is 120px wide in total, has 8px padding, a 1px red border and 12px of space below it.
practice.hint: With border-box, `width: 120px` already includes padding and border.

check.q: Which layer is outside the border?
check.why: Margin is the space outside the border.

check.q: With content-box, width 200px + 10px padding each side. Rendered width (no border)?
check.why: 200 + 10 + 10 = 220px. border-box would keep it at 200px.

lessons.title: Flexbox and responsive basics
lessons.goal: Lay out rows and columns with flexbox and adapt them to phones.
body: `display: flex` lines a container's children up in a row. `justify-content` spaces them along that row (the **main axis**) and `align-items` lines them up across it (the **cross axis**).
`gap` adds space between items, so you don't need margins on each one.
`flex-wrap: wrap` lets items drop to a new line when there isn't room.
A **media query** applies CSS only at certain screen sizes. Write the phone layout first, then add `@media (min-width: 768px)` for bigger screens. That's called **mobile-first**.

demo.say: Turn on flexbox for the container.
On phones, stack the cards vertically.
16px between cards, with no per-card margins.
From 768px wide and up (tablets and desktops)...
...switch to a row, spread the cards out, and center them vertically.

practice.task: Make a navbar: logo on the left, links on the right, vertically centered. On phones, stack the logo above the links.
practice.hint: `justify-content: space-between` pushes the first and last items to the edges.

check.q: Which property spaces items along the main axis?
check.why: justify-content works on the main axis, align-items on the cross axis.

check.q: Mobile-first media queries usually use…
check.why: Start with the phone layout, then add min-width queries for larger screens.

intermediateLessons.title: CSS Grid layouts
intermediateLessons.goal: Build two-dimensional layouts with grid, including auto-fitting card grids.
body: Flexbox lines things up in **one** direction. **Grid** controls rows **and** columns at once.
`grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr` makes a fixed sidebar and a flexible main area. `fr` means "a share of the leftover space".
`repeat(auto-fill, minmax(220px, 1fr))` is the famous responsive card grid: as many 220px+ columns as fit, with no media queries.
`grid-template-areas` names regions so the layout reads like a picture, and it's easy to rearrange for phones.

demo.say: Cards at least 220px wide. The browser fits as many columns as it can, with no breakpoints.

intermediateLessons.title: Custom properties and dark mode
intermediateLessons.goal: Store design values in CSS variables and switch them for dark mode.
body: **Custom properties** (CSS variables) store a value once: `--brand: #87ceeb;`, then `color: var(--brand);`.
Define them on `:root` so the whole page can use them. Change the variable and everything using it updates.
**Dark mode:** redefine the same variables inside `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)`. Components never mention themes; they just use the variables.
`var(--gap, 16px)` gives a fallback value if the variable isn't set.

demo.say: Light theme values, defined once.
When the device is in dark mode, the same names get dark values.
The body reads the variables, so it follows the theme automatically.
The button uses tokens too. `--btn-pad` isn't defined, so the fallback is used.

check.why: var() reads it, with an optional fallback.

intermediateLessons.title: Transitions, keyframes and sticky positioning
intermediateLessons.goal: Animate state changes smoothly and keep a header stuck while scrolling.
body: `transition: transform 200ms ease` animates a property whenever it changes, such as on hover.
`@keyframes` defines a multi-step animation, and `animation:` runs it.
Animate **transform** and **opacity** only. They're cheap for the browser. Animating `width`, `top` or `margin` makes the page recalculate layout every frame, which is slow.
`position: sticky; top: 0;` keeps an element in place once you scroll past it, like a table header or a navbar.
Respect `prefers-reduced-motion`: some people get dizzy from motion.

demo.say: Animate two properties for 200ms whenever they change.
On hover the card lifts. Only transform and shadow change.
A keyframe animation that fades out and back in.
Run it forever, for a loading indicator.
The navbar sticks to the top once you scroll.
People who ask for less motion get none.

check.why: transform and opacity skip layout and paint work.

advancedLessons.title: Cascade layers and a specificity strategy
advancedLessons.goal: Control which CSS wins with @layer and low-specificity selectors.
body: Specificity fights (adding classes or `!important` to win) are a sign of missing structure.
`@layer reset, base, components, utilities;` declares an order. **A later layer beats an earlier one, no matter the specificity** inside them.
Unlayered CSS beats all layers, so put third-party CSS in an early layer to keep it from overriding yours.
`:where()` has **zero** specificity, so base styles wrapped in it are easy to override. `:is()` takes the specificity of its strongest selector.

demo.say: Declare the order once. Later layers win.
Third-party CSS goes in its own early layer, so it can't override your components.
:where() has zero specificity, so these base styles are trivially overridable.
A very specific selector...
...still loses to a single utility class, because utilities is a later layer.

practice.task: Your component library sets `.btn { padding: 12px }` and you can't edit it. Make your `.btn { padding: 8px }` win without !important.
practice.hint: Import the library into an earlier layer.

check.q: Two layers both style .btn. Which wins?
check.why: Layer order beats specificity.

check.q: Specificity of :where(.nav a)?
check.why: :where() is always zero.

advancedLessons.title: Container queries
advancedLessons.goal: Make components respond to the space they're given, not the screen size.
body: Media queries ask "how wide is the **screen**?". But a card in a sidebar and the same card in the main area need different layouts on the same screen.
**Container queries** ask "how wide is my **container**?". Mark a parent with `container-type: inline-size`, then use `@container (min-width: 400px)`.
Name containers (`container-name: card`) when they're nested, so the query targets the right one.
**Container units** like `cqi` (1% of the container's inline size) let type scale with the component.

demo.say: The wrapper becomes a container that children can query.

options: The size of an ancestor marked as a container
check.why: That's the difference from media queries.

check.q: What does container-type: inline-size do?

advancedLessons.title: Animation performance and scroll-driven effects
advancedLessons.goal: Animate at 60fps, and use CSS for effects that used to need JavaScript.
body: The browser draws a frame in steps: **style → layout → paint → composite**. Changing `width` re-runs all of them. Changing `transform` or `opacity` can skip straight to compositing, which happens on the GPU.
`will-change: transform` hints that something will animate. Use it sparingly, only on elements that really animate, because each one costs memory.
Find slow animations in DevTools → Performance: long frames and purple "Layout" blocks are the warning signs.

**Scroll-driven animations** (`animation-timeline: scroll()` or `view()`) tie an animation to scroll position in pure CSS, with no scroll listeners. Wrap them in `@supports` so older browsers just skip the effect.

demo.say: A reading-progress bar. It animates transform: scaleX, never width.
Only browsers that support scroll timelines get the effect.
The bar fills as the page scrolls, with no JavaScript.
Each .reveal fades up as it enters the viewport.
Only transform and opacity: cheap to animate.
And off entirely for people who ask for less motion.

practice.task: A dropdown animates `height` from 0 to auto and stutters. How do you fix it?
practice.hint: Animate a cheap property instead, or use grid-template-rows.

check.q: Which property change only needs compositing?
check.why: transform and opacity skip layout and paint.

check.q: Why wrap scroll-driven animations in @supports?
options: Browsers without support skip the effect cleanly
check.why: Progressive enhancement.

lessons.title: Variables, types and console.log
lessons.goal: Store values with const and let and know the basic types.
body: Use `const` for values that won't be reassigned and `let` for ones that will. Avoid `var`: it has confusing scoping rules.
The basic types are **string** (text), **number**, **boolean** (`true`/`false`), **null** (empty on purpose), **undefined** (not set yet), plus **objects** and **arrays** for groups of values.
`typeof` tells you a value's type. `console.log` prints to the console, which is your main debugging tool.
Compare with `===` (strict equality). `==` converts types first, so `"5" == 5` is true, which hides bugs.

example.output:
string number boolean
Sam has 15 points
false true
2

demo.say: `const`: this name won't be reassigned.
`let` can change. score is now 15.
A boolean, an array and an object.
typeof reports each type.
Read a property with a dot, and join text with +.
Strict equality is false because the types differ. Loose equality converts and says true.
Arrays know their length.

check.why: Strict equality checks the type too: string vs number.

check.q: Which keyword for a value you will reassign?
check.why: let allows reassignment. const doesn't.

lessons.title: Functions and conditionals
lessons.goal: Write functions that take input, make decisions and return output.
body: A **function** is a reusable block of code. It takes **parameters** and **returns** a value.
Arrow functions are a shorter way to write them: `const double = (n) => n * 2;`
`if / else if / else` runs different code depending on a condition. Combine conditions with `&&` (and), `||` (or) and `!` (not).
Keep functions small and **pure** when you can: the same input always gives the same output. Pure functions are the easiest to test.

demo.say: `grade` takes one parameter: score.
The first true condition wins and `return` exits the function.
Only checked if the first condition was false.
The fallback for everything else.
An arrow function that returns a boolean.
95 hits the first branch.
83 fails the first and passes the second.
40 falls through, and isPassing is false.

practice.task: Write `shippingCost(total)`: free if total is 50 or more, otherwise 5.99.
practice.hint: One `if` with an early return is enough.

check.q: What does a function return with no return statement?
check.why: Functions return undefined by default.

check.q: true && false || true evaluates to…
check.why: && runs first: false, then false || true is true.

lessons.title: Arrays and loops: for, map, filter
lessons.goal: Loop over lists and transform them with map and filter.
body: An **array** is an ordered list: `const nums = [3, 8, 1];`. Positions start at **0**, so `nums[0]` is 3.
`for...of` loops over every item. `.push()` adds to the end.
`.map()` makes a **new** array by changing each item. `.filter()` makes a new array keeping only the items that pass a test. Neither changes the original array.
In React you'll use `.map()` constantly to turn data into a list of elements.

demo.say: An array of four numbers.
for...of visits each price and adds it to the running total.
Print the total.
map returns a NEW array with every price times 1.1.
toFixed(2) formats each one to two decimals.
filter keeps only prices under 10. The original still has 4 items.

practice.task: Given `const names = ["ana", "ben", "cy"]`, make a new array of the names in capitals, keeping only those longer than 2 letters.
practice.hint: Chain them: `.filter(...)` then `.map(...)`.

check.q: What does .map() return?
options: A new array of the same length
check.why: map always returns a new array with one result per item.

check.q: [5, 2, 9].filter(n => n > 4) is…
check.why: filter keeps the items whose test returns true.

lessons.title: The DOM and events
lessons.goal: Find elements, change them, and respond to clicks and typing.
body: The **DOM** is the browser's live tree of your HTML. JavaScript reads and changes it.
`document.querySelector(".btn")` finds the first element matching a CSS selector.
Change text with `.textContent`, and toggle classes with `.classList.add/remove/toggle`.
`addEventListener("click", fn)` runs `fn` every time the event happens. Other common events: `input`, `submit`, `keydown`.
In a form's submit handler, call `event.preventDefault()` to stop the page reloading.

demo.say: Two elements: a button, and a span showing the count.
Grab both elements once, at the start.
The count lives in a variable. That's your state.
Listen for clicks on the button.
Each click: add 1 to the count and show it on the page.
Add the `liked` class once the count is above 0, so CSS can restyle the button.

check.why: querySelector takes any CSS selector.

check.why: preventDefault cancels the browser's default action.

intermediateLessons.title: Destructuring, spread and optional chaining
intermediateLessons.goal: Pull values out of objects and arrays, copy them safely, and read nested data without crashing.
body: **Destructuring** unpacks values: `const { name, age } = user;` and `const [first, second] = list;`. You can rename (`{ name: fullName }`) and set defaults (`{ role = "guest" }`).
**Spread** `...` copies: `{ ...user, age: 31 }` makes a new object with one property changed. That's how React state is updated.
**Rest** gathers what's left: `const { password, ...safe } = user;`.
**Optional chaining** `user?.address?.city` returns `undefined` instead of crashing when something in the chain is missing. `??` gives a default only for `null`/`undefined`.

example.output:
Ana guest
30 31
[ 'name', 'age', 'address' ]
No city
a c

demo.say: Unpack name, and give role a default because it's missing.
Spread copies the object and changes age. The original is untouched.
Rest gathers everything except password, which is handy before sending data to the browser.
address is null, so ?. stops safely and ?? supplies the fallback.
Array destructuring. Skip a slot with an empty comma.

practice.hint: `{ ...cart, [id]: qty }`

check.why: Optional chaining stops and returns undefined.

intermediateLessons.title: reduce, find, some, every and sort
intermediateLessons.goal: Summarize and search arrays, and sort them without mutating the original.
body: `reduce` turns an array into **one** value: a total, an object, a grouping. It takes `(accumulator, item) => newAccumulator` and a starting value.
`find` returns the first matching item (or `undefined`). `some` asks "does any match?" and `every` asks "do all match?". Both return a boolean.
`sort` **changes the original array** and compares as strings by default, so `[10, 9, 1].sort()` gives `[1, 10, 9]`. Pass a compare function: `(a, b) => a - b`.
Use `toSorted()` (or `[...arr].sort()`) to get a sorted copy and leave the original alone.

demo.say: Start the sum at 0 and add each total.
find returns the first unpaid order.
Is any total over 80? Are all paid?
toSorted returns a copy, biggest first. The original order is unchanged.
The classic trap: sort without a compare function sorts as text.

practice.task: Use reduce to group `["apple", "avocado", "banana"]` by first letter: `{ a: ["apple", "avocado"], b: ["banana"] }`.
practice.hint: Start with `{}`. For each word, push it into `acc[word[0]]`, creating the array if needed.

check.why: As strings, "100" < "20" < "3". Always pass a compare function for numbers.

check.why: some and every return true or false.

intermediateLessons.title: Promises in depth: parallel requests and errors
intermediateLessons.goal: Run async work in parallel, handle failures, and always clean up.
body: Awaiting requests one after another makes the waits add up. `Promise.all([a(), b()])` runs them **at the same time** and waits for all of them.
`Promise.all` rejects as soon as **one** fails. `Promise.allSettled` waits for all and tells you which succeeded.
`try / catch / finally`: `finally` always runs, so it's where you turn off loading spinners.
Throw your own `Error` with a clear message when something's wrong. Callers catch it in one place.

example.output:
user posts in parallel
[ 'fulfilled', 'rejected' ]
Caught: network down
loading: false

demo.say: A fake request: it resolves or rejects after a delay.
Both 100ms waits run together, so the total is about 100ms, not 200ms.
allSettled reports every result, even the failure.
The awaited promise rejects, so control jumps to catch.
finally runs either way, so loading always ends.

practice.task: Write `withTimeout(promise, ms)` that rejects with "Timed out" if the promise takes longer than ms.
practice.hint: `Promise.race` with a promise that rejects after ms.

check.q: Promise.all with one rejected promise…
check.why: all rejects on the first failure. Use allSettled to get every result.

check.q: Where should you stop a loading spinner?
check.why: finally runs on success and on failure.

advancedLessons.title: The event loop, microtasks and timers
advancedLessons.goal: Predict the order async code runs in, and avoid blocking the page.
body: JavaScript runs on **one thread**. While your code runs, the page can't respond. Long tasks cause jank.

The **event loop**: run the current script to the end, then run **all microtasks** (Promise callbacks, `await` continuations, `queueMicrotask`), then take **one macrotask** (a `setTimeout` callback, an event), and repeat.
So a `Promise.then` always runs before a `setTimeout(fn, 0)` that was scheduled earlier.
Break up heavy work (yield with `await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r))` between chunks), or move it to a **Web Worker**.

example.output:
1 script start
2 async fn starts (sync part)
3 script end
4 promise 1
4b microtask
4c after await
5 promise 2
6 timeout

demo.say: Synchronous code runs first, top to bottom.
A timer is a macrotask. It waits until the stack AND the microtask queue are empty.
These callbacks are microtasks, queued in order.
An async function runs synchronously until its first await.
The script ends.
Now all microtasks run, in the order they were queued.
The chained .then was queued by the first one, so it runs next.
Finally, the timer.

practice.task: Predict the output: `setTimeout(() => log("A")); Promise.resolve().then(() => log("B")); log("C");`
practice.hint: Synchronous code, then microtasks, then timers.

check.q: Which runs first after the script finishes?
check.why: All microtasks run before the next macrotask.

check.q: A 2-second loop in a click handler will…
check.why: One thread: nothing else runs until it finishes.

advancedLessons.title: Prototypes, classes and private fields
advancedLessons.goal: Understand what classes really are, and write classes with real encapsulation.
body: Every object has a **prototype**: another object it falls back to when a property is missing. Methods live on the prototype, shared by every instance.
`class` is cleaner syntax over prototypes. `extends` links one prototype to another.
`#private` fields can't be read or changed from outside the class. That's real privacy, enforced by the language (unlike the old `_underscore` convention).
`get` and `set` make computed properties, and `static` members belong to the class itself, not to instances.

demo.say: A private field: only code inside the class can touch it.
A static counter lives on the class, not on each timer.
Returning this allows chaining: .tick().tick().
A getter reads like a property but computes its value.
extends links the prototypes, and super() runs the parent constructor.
125 + 5 seconds is 2:10, and one timer was created.
Under the hood, classes are prototypes.
The private field is invisible, and tick lives on the prototype, not on the object.

practice.task: Write a `BankAccount` class with a private #balance, a deposit method that rejects non-positive amounts, and a read-only `balance` getter.
practice.hint: Throw an Error in deposit for amounts <= 0.

check.q: Where do class methods live?
check.why: Instances share methods through the prototype.

check.q: obj.#secret from outside the class…
check.why: Private fields can't even be written about outside the class.

advancedLessons.title: Debounce, throttle and memoize
advancedLessons.goal: Write the three utility functions interviewers ask about most, and know when to use each.
body: **Debounce**: wait until calls **stop** for N ms, then run once. Use it for search-as-you-type and window resize.
**Throttle**: run at most once every N ms, however often it's called. Use it for scroll and mousemove handlers.
**Memoize**: cache results by input, so repeated calls with the same arguments are instant. Use it for expensive pure functions.
All three are **closures**: an inner function that remembers variables (a timer, the last run time, a cache) from the outer function after it has returned.

demo.say: Debounce: each call cancels the previous timer, so only the last one survives the pause.
Throttle: remember when it last ran, and ignore calls that come too soon.
Memoize: check the cache, and compute only on a miss.
Five scroll events in a row, but only the first one runs.
The second call came from the cache.
Four keystrokes, one search, 50ms after the last.

practice.hint: Attach a function to the returned function: `debounced.cancel = () => clearTimeout(timer)`.

check.why: Wait until typing pauses.

check.q: What makes these utilities work?
check.why: The returned function remembers the timer or cache.

lessons.title: What an API is: HTTP and JSON
lessons.goal: Read an HTTP request and response and parse JSON.
body: An **API** is a way for one program to ask another for data or actions. On the web, that conversation happens over **HTTP**.

Your code sends a **request**: a **method** (`GET` to read, `POST` to create, `PUT`/`PATCH` to update, `DELETE` to remove) and a **URL** (the endpoint). The server sends back a **response** with a **status code** and usually a **JSON** body.
Status codes in short: **2xx** worked (200 OK, 201 Created), **4xx** your request was wrong (400 Bad Request, 401 not logged in, 404 Not Found), **5xx** the server broke.
**JSON** is text shaped like JavaScript objects. `JSON.parse` turns text into an object, and `JSON.stringify` turns an object into text.

demo.say: This is what a response body looks like: plain text in JSON format.
JSON.parse turns it into a real object you can read.
JSON.stringify turns an object into text, ready to send in a POST body.
Text in, object out.

practice.task: Which method and status would you expect when: (a) loading a user profile, (b) creating a new post, (c) asking for a user that doesn't exist?

lessons.title: fetch with async/await
lessons.goal: Request data with fetch, check for errors, and use the JSON.
body: `fetch(url)` returns a **Promise**: a value that arrives later. `await` pauses the function until it arrives. You can only use `await` inside an `async` function (or at the top level of a module).
**fetch does not throw on 404 or 500.** It only throws when the network fails. Always check `response.ok` yourself.
`await response.json()` reads and parses the body.
Wrap it all in `try/catch` so one failed request doesn't crash your app.

demo.say: `async` lets this function use `await`.
Send a GET request and wait for the response.
fetch won't throw on 404, so check `ok` yourself and throw.
Read the JSON body and return it.
Network or status errors land here. Return null so callers can handle it.
An async function returns a Promise, so use .then() or await to get the value.

check.why: fetch only rejects on network failure. Check response.ok.

check.q: Where can you use await?
options: Inside async functions (or module top level)
check.why: await needs an async context.

lessons.title: axios: a friendlier HTTP client
lessons.goal: Make GET and POST requests with axios and handle its errors.
body: **axios** is a popular library that wraps HTTP requests. Install it with `npm install axios`.
Differences from fetch: axios **parses JSON for you** (it's in `response.data`), and it **throws on 4xx and 5xx** responses, so `try/catch` catches HTTP errors too.
`params` builds the query string for you, and the second argument to `axios.post` is the body, sent as JSON.
Both work. fetch needs no install. axios saves boilerplate and adds features like interceptors.

demo.say: Import axios after installing it.

Three posts came back.

check.why: axios puts the parsed JSON in response.data.

check.q: axios gets a 500. What happens?

intermediateLessons.title: Query strings, headers and POST bodies
intermediateLessons.goal: Build URLs safely and send JSON with the right headers.
body: `URLSearchParams` builds query strings and escapes spaces and symbols for you. Never glue user input into a URL by hand.
**Headers** carry information about the request: `Content-Type: application/json` says the body is JSON, and `Authorization: Bearer <token>` proves who you are.
To POST JSON with fetch, set the method and that header, and `JSON.stringify` the body.
Check `response.ok` before reading the body, and read error details from it when there are some.

intermediateLessons.title: Loading, error and empty states
intermediateLessons.goal: Model every state a request can be in, so the UI never shows a blank screen.
body: A request isn't just "have data". It's **idle**, **loading**, **success**, **empty** (success but nothing to show) or **error**.
Track one `status` string instead of several booleans. `isLoading` and `isError` both true at once is a bug waiting to happen.
Each state gets its own UI: a skeleton for loading, a friendly message with a retry for error, and a helpful nudge for empty.
This pattern carries straight into React state.

intermediateLessons.title: API keys, axios instances and interceptors
intermediateLessons.goal: Keep keys out of your code and configure axios once for a whole app.
body: **Never commit API keys.** Put them in `.env.local` (and add it to `.gitignore`), then read them with `process.env.MY_KEY`.

Anything sent to the browser can be read by anyone. In Next.js, only variables starting with `NEXT_PUBLIC_` reach the browser. **Secret keys belong on the server only**, so call the API from a server component or route handler.
`axios.create({ baseURL, timeout, headers })` makes a configured client, so every call shares the same settings.
**Interceptors** run on every request or response. Use them to add an auth token, or to turn every error into one friendly message.

demo.say: One client with the base URL and an 8-second timeout.
Every request gets the token from the environment, never from the code.
Successful responses pass straight through.
Every failure becomes one clear message, written in one place.
Callers stay tiny: a path plus params.

practice.task: Write the .env.local and .gitignore lines for a TMDB token, and say where in Next.js the searchMovies call should run.
practice.hint: Secret token, so not NEXT_PUBLIC_.

solution.code:
# .env.local
TMDB_TOKEN=eyJhbGciOi...

# .gitignore
.env*.local

Call searchMovies from a server component or a route handler (app/api/search/route.js), never from a "use client" file.

check.q: A NEXT_PUBLIC_ variable is…
options: Visible to anyone using the site
check.why: It's bundled into browser code.

check.q: What's a good use for a response interceptor?
options: Turning every HTTP error into one friendly message
check.why: It runs for every response, so error handling lives in one place.

advancedLessons.title: Cancelling requests and retrying with backoff
advancedLessons.goal: Make network code that survives slow and flaky servers.
body: `AbortController` cancels a request: pass `controller.signal` to fetch, and call `controller.abort()`. Use it when a user leaves the page or types a new search.
`AbortSignal.timeout(5000)` gives you a signal that aborts on its own after 5 seconds.
**Retry** only what can succeed on a second try: network errors, 429 (rate limited) and 5xx. **Never** retry a 400 or 404; it will fail the same way.
Wait longer between each try (**exponential backoff**: 200ms, 400ms, 800ms…) plus a little randomness (**jitter**), so many clients don't retry at the same instant.

example.output:
attempt 1 failed, retrying
attempt 2 failed, retrying
succeeded with 200 after 3 tries

demo.say: Every attempt gives up after 5 seconds.
Success: return immediately.
Only 429 and 5xx are worth retrying. A 404 fails right away.
Don't retry client errors that came through as exceptions either.
Exponential backoff with jitter: about 100ms, then 200ms, then 400ms.
A fake server that fails twice with 503, then works.
demo.out:
attempt 1 failed, retrying
attempt 2 failed, retrying
succeeded with 200 after 3 tries

practice.task: In a React search component, cancel the previous request whenever the query changes.
practice.hint: New AbortController in the effect, abort in the cleanup, ignore AbortError.

check.q: Which response should you retry?
check.why: 5xx and 429 may succeed later. 4xx won't.

check.q: Why add jitter to backoff?
options: So many clients don't retry at the same moment
check.why: It spreads retries out instead of hammering the server together.

advancedLessons.title: Caching and stale-while-revalidate
advancedLessons.goal: Serve data instantly from a cache while refreshing it in the background.
body: **HTTP caching** is controlled by the server's `Cache-Control` header: `max-age=60` (fresh for 60s), `no-store` (never cache), `stale-while-revalidate=300` (serve stale for 5 more minutes while refreshing).
**Stale-while-revalidate (SWR)**: show cached data immediately, fetch fresh data in the background, then update. It's the idea behind SWR and TanStack Query.
**Deduplicate** in-flight requests: if three components ask for the same thing at once, make one request and share the promise.
Cache **keys** must include everything that changes the answer (URL, query, user).

example.output:
books v1 books v1 requests: 1
books v1
books v2

demo.say: Two maps: finished results, and requests still in flight.
Only one request per key at a time. Everyone else shares its promise.
Nothing cached yet: wait for the network.
Cached but old: return it NOW, and refresh in the background.
Two simultaneous callers, one request.
After the TTL: you still get v1 instantly, while v2 loads behind the scenes.
Next call: the fresh data.

practice.task: What Cache-Control header suits: (a) a hashed JS file like app.3f9a1.js, (b) a user's account page, (c) a product list that updates hourly?
practice.hint: Hashed files never change. Account pages are private.

solution.code:
(a) public, max-age=31536000, immutable
(b) private, no-store
(c) public, max-age=300, stale-while-revalidate=3600

check.q: What does stale-while-revalidate do?
options: Serves cached data now and refreshes in the background
check.why: Instant response, eventual freshness.

check.q: Why deduplicate in-flight requests?
options: Avoid sending the same request many times at once
check.why: Several components often need the same data at the same time.

advancedLessons.title: CORS explained, and designing for rate limits
advancedLessons.goal: Understand why the browser blocks some requests, and handle 429 responses well.
body: The **same-origin policy**: a page can only read responses from its own origin (scheme + host + port). `https://app.com` and `https://api.app.com` are **different** origins.
**CORS** lets a server opt in: `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.com`. CORS is enforced by the **browser**; curl and servers ignore it. That's why "it works in Postman" proves nothing.
Requests with JSON bodies or custom headers trigger a **preflight**: an `OPTIONS` request asking permission first.
**Rate limits**: APIs answer `429 Too Many Requests`, often with `Retry-After`. Respect it, debounce user-triggered calls, and cache.

demo.say: A cross-origin POST with JSON, which needs a preflight.
The browser asks first: may this origin send a POST with this header?
The server's answer. Without it, the browser blocks the response (the request may still have reached the server!).
On 429, read Retry-After and tell the user, instead of retrying in a tight loop.

practice.task: Your React app on localhost:5173 gets a CORS error calling your Express API on localhost:3000. Give two fixes.
practice.hint: One on the server, one in the dev setup.

solution.code:
1. Server: app.use(cors({ origin: "http://localhost:5173" }))
2. Dev proxy: in vite.config, server.proxy: { "/api": "http://localhost:3000" }, then call /api/... from the same origin.
(In production, serve both from one origin, or set CORS to your real domain.)

check.q: Who enforces CORS?
check.why: That's why curl and Postman never show CORS errors.

check.q: http://localhost:3000 vs http://localhost:5173 are…
options: Same if on the same machine
check.why: The port is part of the origin.

lessons.title: Why TypeScript, and basic types
lessons.goal: Add type annotations and read a type error.
body: TypeScript is JavaScript plus **types**. A checker reads your code **before** it runs and flags mistakes like passing a string where a number is expected.
Annotate with a colon: `let age: number = 30;`. Often you don't need to, because TypeScript **infers** the type from the value.
Basic types: `string`, `number`, `boolean`, arrays like `string[]`, and `any` (switches checking off, so avoid it).
A **union** like `string | null` means "one of these".
TypeScript files end in `.ts` (or `.tsx` with JSX). They're compiled to plain JavaScript.

demo.say: An explicit annotation: username must be a string.
No annotation needed: TypeScript infers number from 40.
An array of strings.
Parameters and the return value are typed.
A union: nickname can be a string or null.
Runs like normal JavaScript.
Uncomment this and the checker stops you before the code ever runs.

practice.hint: Use `amount.toFixed(2)`.

check.q: What does `any` do?
options: Turns off type checking for that value
check.why: any skips checking, so avoid it when you can.

check.q: When does TypeScript catch type errors?
check.why: Type checking happens before the code runs.

lessons.title: Typing objects with interfaces
lessons.goal: Describe object shapes with interfaces and optional properties.
body: An **interface** describes the shape of an object: which properties it has and their types.
A `?` marks a property as **optional**: `bio?: string`.
`readonly` stops a property being changed after creation.
Interfaces make editor autocomplete work, and they catch typos like `user.emial`.

demo.say: The User shape: id can't be changed, and bio is optional.
greet only accepts objects with this shape.
bio may be missing, so check it before using it.
Valid with no bio, because it's optional.
An array of User objects.

check.q: What does `bio?: string` mean?
check.why: ? makes the property optional.

check.q: What does readonly prevent?
check.why: readonly blocks reassignment.

intermediateLessons.title: Union types and narrowing
intermediateLessons.goal: Describe values that can be one of several types, and narrow them safely.
body: A **union** says a value is one of several types: `string | number`, or literal values like `"loading" | "success" | "error"`.
Before using a union, **narrow** it: `typeof x === "string"`, `Array.isArray(x)`, `"key" in obj`, or checking a shared property. Inside the check, TypeScript knows the exact type.
**Discriminated unions** share a literal property (like `status`) and are the best way to model request state: each status carries exactly the data it needs.
`never` in a `default` branch makes TypeScript warn you when you forget a case.

demo.say: Three shapes, told apart by the status literal.
Inside case "success", TypeScript knows data exists.
And here it knows message exists. Using r.data would be a type error.
If someone adds a new status and forgets a case, this line fails to compile.
typeof narrows a primitive union.
Each call takes the right branch.

practice.task: Model a `Shape` union of circle (radius) and rect (width, height) with a `kind` property, and write `area(s: Shape)`.
practice.hint: `type Shape = { kind: "circle"; radius: number } | { kind: "rect"; width: number; height: number }`

check.q: What is narrowing?
options: Making a type smaller in memory
Checking a value so TypeScript knows its exact type
check.why: Checks like typeof or a discriminant narrow a union.

check.q: Why the `never` default?
options: Compile error if a case is forgotten
check.why: Only an impossible value fits never.

intermediateLessons.title: Generics
intermediateLessons.goal: Write functions and types that work for any type, while staying type-safe.
body: A **generic** is a type parameter, like a function argument but for types: `function first<T>(items: T[]): T | undefined`.
TypeScript usually **infers** T from what you pass in: `first([1, 2])` returns `number | undefined`.
You see generics everywhere: `Array<string>`, `Promise<User>`, `useState<number>(0)`.
`<T extends { id: string }>` **constrains** T: any type is fine as long as it has an id.

demo.say: T is whatever type the array holds. The return type follows it.
A generic interface: the response shape is the same, and the data type varies.
A constraint: T can be anything that has an id string.
T is inferred as number.
book is typed { id, title }, so book.title autocompletes.
All three are fully typed.

practice.task: Write a generic `groupBy<T>(items: T[], key: (item: T) => string): Record<string, T[]>`.
practice.hint: Like the reduce grouping exercise, with types added.

check.q: In first<T>(items: T[]), what decides T?
check.why: TypeScript infers T from what you pass.

check.q: <T extends { id: string }> means…
options: T must at least have an id string
check.why: extends constrains T to types with that shape.

intermediateLessons.title: Typing React components and API data
intermediateLessons.goal: Type props, state, events and fetched JSON in a React + TypeScript project.
body: Type props with an interface, and destructure them in the parameters: `function Card({ title }: CardProps)`.
`useState` infers simple types. For empty starting values, pass the type: `useState<User | null>(null)`.
Events have types too: `React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>` and `React.FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>`.

**JSON from an API is untrusted.** `await res.json()` is `any`. Give it a type, but remember that types don't check the data at runtime. For important data, validate it (with a schema library like Zod, in Advanced).

demo.say: The shape of one book from the API.
Props: an optional author filter and a callback that receives a Book.
An empty array needs a type, or TypeScript guesses never[].
Tell TypeScript what the JSON is. Remember this isn't checked at runtime.
A typed event: e.target.value is known to be a string.
onPick(b) type-checks because b is a Book.

practice.hint: `interface ButtonProps extends React.ButtonHTMLAttributes<HTMLButtonElement> { variant?: "primary" | "ghost" }`

check.q: useState([]) with no type gives…
check.why: An empty literal infers never[], so pass a type.

check.q: Does `as Book[]` check the JSON at runtime?
options: No, it's only a promise to the compiler
check.why: Types disappear at runtime. Validate data you don't control.

advancedLessons.title: Utility types
advancedLessons.goal: Derive new types from existing ones instead of copying them.
body: Copy-pasted types drift apart. Derive them instead, so one change updates everything.
`Partial<T>` makes every property optional (good for update payloads). `Required<T>` does the opposite.
`Pick<T, "a" | "b">` keeps some properties, and `Omit<T, "password">` removes some.
`Record<K, V>` types a dictionary. `ReturnType<typeof fn>` and `Awaited<T>` pull types out of functions and promises.

demo.say: Everything except password, so it's safe to send to the browser.
Only name and email, and both optional: a PATCH body.
User["role"] reads a property's type. Record makes a key for each role.
The return type guarantees password can't sneak out.
Pull the resolved type out of a function: no copying.
Every value is checked against a derived type.

practice.task: Create a `NewUser` type for a sign-up form: everything in User except id and role.
practice.hint: Omit with a union of keys.

check.q: Partial<T> makes…
check.why: Useful for update payloads.

check.q: Omit<User, "password"> is…
check.why: Omit removes keys.

advancedLessons.title: Mapped types, conditional types and satisfies
advancedLessons.goal: Write your own type helpers, and check object literals without losing their exact types.
body: A **mapped type** loops over keys: `{ [K in keyof T]: ... }`. All the built-in utility types are written this way.
A **conditional type** chooses a type: `T extends string ? "text" : "other"`. `infer` captures part of a type inside the condition.
**Template literal types** build string types from other types, e.g. turning the key "theme" into "getTheme" (see line 1 below).
`satisfies` checks that a value matches a type **without** widening it, so you keep the exact keys and literal values for autocomplete.

demo.say: A mapped type with key renaming: each key K becomes getK, returning T[K].
infer captures the element type of an array.
SettingsGetters is { getTheme(): "light" | "dark"; getFontSize(): number }.
satisfies: every value must start with /, but routes.lesson keeps its exact literal type.
Tag is "html" | "css".
All of it type-checks, and it runs like plain JavaScript.

practice.task: Write `Nullable<T>`, which makes every property of T also accept null.
practice.hint: A mapped type: [K in keyof T]: T[K] | null

check.q: What does `satisfies` do differently from a type annotation?
options: Checks the type but keeps the value's exact inferred type
check.why: An annotation widens to the annotated type; satisfies doesn't.

check.q: { [K in keyof T]: string } is a…
check.why: It maps over T's keys.

advancedLessons.title: Strict mode and runtime validation with Zod
advancedLessons.goal: Turn on the strict compiler settings, and validate untrusted data at runtime.
body: Turn on `"strict": true` in tsconfig.json. It enables `strictNullChecks` (no forgetting null), `noImplicitAny`, and more. Also worth adding: `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` (array[i] may be undefined).
Types vanish at runtime. Data from APIs, forms, URLs and localStorage can be **anything**.
**Zod** describes a shape once, and gives you both a runtime validator and a TypeScript type (`z.infer`).
`safeParse` returns `{ success, data }` or `{ success: false, error }`, so you never trust raw input.

demo.say: Describe the shape once, with friendly messages.
coerce turns form strings like "30" into numbers.
The TypeScript type comes FROM the schema, so they can never disagree.
Input is unknown, which is honest about where it came from. safeParse never throws.
Valid input is trimmed and converted.
Invalid input gives readable errors per field.
demo.out: [ 'name: Name must be at least 2 characters', 'email: Enter a valid email' ]

practice.hint: `z.array(BookSchema).parse(await res.json())`

check.q: Why validate at runtime if you have TypeScript?
options: Types disappear at runtime; outside data can be anything
check.why: The compiler can't see what an API actually sends.

check.q: z.infer<typeof Schema> gives you…
options: The TypeScript type matching the schema
check.why: One source of truth for type and validation.

lessons.title: Utility classes and setup
lessons.goal: Style an element entirely with Tailwind utility classes.
body: Tailwind gives you small single-purpose classes: `p-4` (padding), `text-xl` (font size), `bg-sky-400` (background), `rounded-lg` (corners). You combine them in your HTML instead of writing CSS.
The spacing scale steps by 4px: `p-1` is 4px, `p-4` is 16px, `p-8` is 32px.
Colors use a name and a shade: `bg-red-500`, `text-yellow-300`. Lower numbers are lighter.
Setup in a Vite or Next.js project (Tailwind v4): install `tailwindcss` and its plugin, then add `@import "tailwindcss";` to your main CSS file. Next.js's create-next-app can set it up for you.

lessons.title: Responsive design and states
lessons.goal: Use breakpoint and state prefixes like md: and hover:.
body: Prefix a class with a breakpoint to apply it only from that width up: `md:flex-row` means "from 768px up". Tailwind is mobile-first, so un-prefixed classes are the phone styles.
Breakpoints: `sm` 640px, `md` 768px, `lg` 1024px, `xl` 1280px.
State prefixes apply on interaction: `hover:`, `focus-visible:`, `disabled:`. Always give keyboard users a `focus-visible:` style.
`dark:` applies when the user's system is in dark mode.

intermediateLessons.title: Customizing the theme and dark mode
intermediateLessons.goal: Add your own colors and fonts to Tailwind and support a manual dark mode.
body: In Tailwind v4, customize in CSS with `@theme`. Adding `--color-sun: #ffd23f;` creates `bg-sun`, `text-sun`, `border-sun` and the rest.
`--font-display: "Archivo", sans-serif;` creates the `font-display` class.

`dark:` follows the device setting by default. For a **toggle**, define a custom variant that reads a `data-theme` attribute: `@custom-variant dark (&:where([data-theme=dark], [data-theme=dark] *));`.
Better still: point theme colors at CSS variables and swap the variables, so most components need no `dark:` classes at all.

dark: now follows data-theme on <html>, so your toggle controls it.
The color values live in variables, with dark versions.
bg-bg and text-ink read the variables, so they switch with the theme on their own.
Brand colors and a display font become utilities: bg-sun, font-display.

check.q: Why point theme colors at CSS variables?

intermediateLessons.title: Reusing styles without the mess
intermediateLessons.goal: Know when to make a component, when to use @apply, and how to keep long class lists readable.
body: Repeated class lists are a sign you need a **component** (a React component or a partial template), not a CSS class. The component is the reuse.
`@apply` copies utilities into a CSS class. It's fine for things you can't wrap in a component, like styling raw HTML from a CMS, but overusing it brings back the problems Tailwind solves.
Keep variants in an object and pick from it, rather than building class names with string pieces: Tailwind only finds **complete** class names in your files, so `bg-${color}-500` never works.
Arbitrary values (`top-[117px]`, `bg-[#bada55]`) are for one-offs. If you repeat one, add it to the theme.

demo.say: Each variant is a complete, literal class list, so Tailwind can find every class.
The component is the reuse. Anyone can use <Button variant="ghost">.
Shared base classes plus the variant, plus any extras passed in.
Building class names from pieces fails silently: the CSS is never generated.

check.q: Why doesn't `bg-${color}-500` work?
options: Tailwind only generates classes it finds written out in full
check.why: Tailwind scans your files for complete class names.

check.q: Best way to reuse a long button class list?
check.why: Components are Tailwind's unit of reuse.

advancedLessons.title: A design system on Tailwind
advancedLessons.goal: Turn brand decisions into tokens and component recipes that a whole team can follow.
body: A design system is **decisions written down**: the colors, type scale, spacing, radii and components everyone uses.
Put **semantic** tokens in `@theme` (`--color-surface`, `--color-danger`), not just raw palette names, so code says what a color is for.
Component **recipes** keep variants in one place: base classes plus variant and size maps. Libraries like `cva` formalize this.
When classes are merged from outside (a `className` prop), use `tailwind-merge` so `p-2` passed in correctly replaces a default `p-4` instead of both applying.

demo.say: Semantic tokens: what a color is FOR, not just what it looks like.
Base classes every button shares, including focus and disabled states.
Variants are complete class strings, so Tailwind can find them.
Sizes are separate from variants, so any combination works.

lessons.title: Components and JSX
lessons.goal: Write function components that return JSX.
body: A React **component** is a function that returns **JSX**: HTML-like syntax inside JavaScript. Component names start with a **capital letter**.
JSX rules: return **one** parent element (or a fragment `<>...`), use `className` instead of `class`, close every tag (``), and put JavaScript inside `{ }`.
You build a page by nesting components, like `<App>` containing `<Header>` and `<ProductList>`. That's the **component tree**.
Start a project with `npm create vite@latest` (React template) or with Next.js.

Normal JavaScript can sit above the return.

Use your component like a tag.

lessons.goal: Make components reusable by passing them props.
body: **Props** are a component's inputs, passed like HTML attributes: `<PlantCard name="Fern" price={12} />`.
Inside, props arrive as one object. Destructure them: `function PlantCard({ name, price })`.
Data flows **down**: parents pass props to children. A child never changes its props.
`children` is a special prop: whatever you put between the opening and closing tags.

lessons.title: State and events with useState
lessons.goal: Store changing data in state and update it from events.
body: **State** is data a component remembers between renders. `const [count, setCount] = useState(0);` gives you the current value and a setter function.
Calling the setter **re-renders** the component with the new value. Never change state directly (`count++` won't update the screen).
Events use camelCase and receive a function: `onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}`.
When the new value depends on the old one, pass a function: `setCount((c) => c + 1)`. It always uses the latest value.

Two pieces of state: a number and a boolean.
A functional update: change the count based on the previous one.

lessons.title: Rendering lists with keys
lessons.goal: Turn an array into elements with map and give each a stable key.
body: Use `.map()` to turn an array of data into an array of JSX elements.
Each element needs a **key** prop that is unique and stable, usually the item's id. React uses keys to know which item is which when the list changes.
Avoid using the array index as the key when items can be added, removed or re-ordered. It causes subtle bugs, like the wrong item keeping its typed input.
Combine with `.filter()` to show only some items.

intermediateLessons.title: useEffect, cleanup and fetching data
intermediateLessons.goal: Sync a component with the outside world and clean up after yourself.
body: `useEffect(fn, deps)` runs **after** React draws the screen. Use it to sync with things outside React: timers, subscriptions, the document title, and fetching data.
The **dependency array** says when to re-run: `[]` runs once on mount, and `[id]` runs again whenever id changes. Leaving the array out runs it after every render, which is usually a bug.
Return a **cleanup** function to undo the effect: clear the timer, remove the listener, cancel the request. React runs it before the next run and on unmount.
When fetching, ignore stale responses: if the id changes mid-request, the old answer must not overwrite the new one. An `ignore` flag or an `AbortController` handles it.
Don't use effects for things you can calculate during render (filtered lists, totals).

demo.say: Each run makes its own AbortController.
Fetch, check ok, parse, store.
An abort isn't a real error, so ignore it.
Cleanup: if id changes or the component unmounts, cancel the old request.
Re-run whenever id changes.
A second effect syncs the browser tab title with state.
Render each state: error, loading, success.

check.why: No array means every render, which is rarely what you want.

options: Undoing the effect: timers, listeners, requests

intermediateLessons.title: Controlled forms and lifting state up
intermediateLessons.goal: Build a validated form, and share state between sibling components.
body: A **controlled input** gets its `value` from state and updates it in `onChange`. React is the one source of truth.
Keep form values in one object: `const [form, setForm] = useState({ name: "", email: "" })`, and update with spread and the input's `name`.
Validate on submit (and optionally on blur). Show errors next to fields, connected with `aria-describedby`.
**Lifting state up:** when two siblings need the same data, move the state to their closest shared parent and pass it down as props, along with functions to change it.

demo.say: Validation is a pure function, which makes it easy to test.
One state object for every field, plus one for errors.
One change handler for all inputs, using each input's name.
On submit: validate, show the errors, and only continue when there are none.
value comes from state. The error is linked and announced.
onDone is lifted state: the parent decides what happens next.

intermediateLessons.title: Context and custom hooks
intermediateLessons.goal: Share state across the tree without prop drilling, and package logic in reusable hooks.
body: **Prop drilling** is passing props through components that don't use them. **Context** lets any component below a Provider read a value directly.
Pattern: `createContext`, a Provider component that owns the state, and a `useX()` hook that reads the context and throws a clear error when used outside the Provider.
Context is for app-wide things that change rarely: theme, signed-in user, cart. For fast-changing or complex state, look at Redux Toolkit or Zustand (Advanced).
A **custom hook** is a function starting with `use` that calls other hooks. It shares *logic*, not state: each component calling it gets its own copy.

demo.say: Create the context. null means "no provider found".
The Provider owns the state and shares both the value and the way to change it.
A guard hook: a clear error beats a mysterious undefined.
A custom hook works like useState, but saves to localStorage, with try/catch because storage can fail.
Any component under the Provider reads the theme directly. No drilling.

check.why: Hooks share logic. Context shares state.

check.q: Context is a good fit for…
check.why: Rarely-changing, widely-used values.

advancedLessons.title: useReducer and state machines
advancedLessons.goal: Move complex state logic into a pure reducer, and make impossible states impossible.
body: When several pieces of state change together, or the next state depends on the previous one in complicated ways, use `useReducer(reducer, initialState)`.
A **reducer** is a pure function `(state, action) => newState`. All the update logic lives in one place, and you can unit-test it without React.
Components just `dispatch({ type: "added", text })`. They say *what happened*, not how to update.
Thinking in **states** (idle → submitting → success | error) rather than booleans is a **state machine**. Each action is only allowed from certain states, which stops bugs like submitting twice.

demo.say: One state object with a status, instead of isLoading/isError/isDone booleans.
You can't change the cart while a payment is in progress.
Submitting twice, or with an empty cart, does nothing. The double-click bug is impossible.
Unknown actions fail loudly during development.

The second submit is ignored too.
A failure moves to error and keeps the message for the UI.

practice.hint: Check state.status === "error" first.

check.q: What must a reducer be?
options: Pure: same input, same output, no side effects
check.why: Purity makes it predictable and testable.

check.q: Why model state as a status string?
options: Impossible combinations of booleans can't happen
check.why: A state machine is always in exactly one state.

advancedLessons.title: React performance: memo, useMemo, useCallback and the compiler
advancedLessons.goal: Find real slowdowns, and know which tools fix which problem.
body: **Measure first.** React DevTools → Profiler shows which components rendered and how long they took. Don't optimize guesses.
A component re-renders when its parent re-renders, even if its props didn't change. `memo(Component)` skips the render when the props are the same.

`memo` compares props **by reference**, so new objects or functions created each render break it. `useMemo` keeps an object (or an expensive calculation) stable, and `useCallback` keeps a function stable.
The **React Compiler** (on in many new Next.js projects) adds this memoization automatically. With it, you rarely write these hooks by hand.
Other big wins: **virtualize** long lists (only render what's visible), and keep fast-changing state low in the tree.

demo.say: memo: Row only re-renders when its props change.
useMemo: the filtered list is recalculated only when items or filter change.
useCallback: the same toggle function every render, so memo(Row) can do its job.
The functional update means toggle never needs `items` as a dependency.
Typing in the filter re-renders TodoList, but unchanged rows are skipped.

practice.task: A memo'd `Chart` still re-renders on every keystroke. Its parent passes `options={{ color: "red" }}`. Why, and what's the fix?
practice.hint: Object identity.

check.q: What should you do before optimizing?
check.why: Optimize what's actually slow.

check.q: memo fails when you pass…
options: A new inline object or function each render
check.why: Props are compared by reference.

advancedLessons.title: Global state with Redux Toolkit
advancedLessons.goal: Know when an app needs a global store, and build one with Redux Toolkit.
body: Reach for a store when many distant components read and change the same data, and Context re-renders too much. Examples: a cart, a signed-in user with permissions, a multi-step editor.
**Redux Toolkit** (RTK) is the modern way to write Redux. `createSlice` makes the reducer and the action creators together.
Inside a slice reducer you can "mutate" `state` directly. RTK uses Immer to turn that into a safe immutable update.
Components read with `useSelector((s) => s.cart.items)` and update with `dispatch(addItem(...))`. Derived values (totals, counts) are computed in selectors, not stored.
Lighter options: **Zustand** (a tiny store) and **TanStack Query** for server data (which shouldn't live in Redux at all).

demo.say: A slice: a name, a starting state, and its reducers.
It looks like mutation, but Immer produces a new state object.
Action creators are generated for you.
configureStore adds the dev tools and safety checks.
A selector derives the count. Never store values you can calculate.
Two ferns; the cactus was added then removed.
The old state is untouched (immutable), and actions are named slice/reducer.

check.why: RTK wraps reducers with Immer.

check.why: Derived data stays in sync automatically.

lessons.title: What Next.js adds, and file-based routing
lessons.goal: Create pages by creating folders in the app directory.
body: Next.js is a **framework** on top of React. It adds routing, server rendering, image optimization and an easy deploy.
Create a project with `npx create-next-app@latest`. Pages live in the **`app/` folder**.
**The folder path is the URL.** `app/page.js` is `/`, and `app/about/page.js` is `/about`. A folder only becomes a route when it has a `page.js` file.
Each `page.js` default-exports a React component.

lessons.title: Server and client components

Add `"use client"` at the top of a file when the component needs **the browser**: `useState`, `useEffect`, `onClick` and other event handlers, or `window` and `localStorage`.
**Keep client components small** and push them down the tree. A server page can render a small client `<LikeButton />`.
A server component can fetch with `await` right in the component. No `useEffect` and no loading state are needed for the first render.

advancedLessons.title: Caching, revalidation and streaming
advancedLessons.goal: Control exactly when Next.js data is fresh, and stream slow parts of a page.
body: Tag cached data with `fetch(url, { next: { tags: ["books"] } })`. After data changes, call `revalidateTag("books", "max")` in a Server Action or route handler. The next visitor gets stale data instantly while fresh data loads in the background.
In Next.js 16, `revalidateTag` takes a second argument (a cache profile). `"max"` is the recommended one. Use `updateTag` in a Server Action when the user must see their own change immediately.
`revalidatePath("/books")` refreshes everything on a route.
**Streaming:** wrap a slow component in `<Suspense fallback={...}>`. The rest of the page is sent at once, and the slow part streams in when ready.

advancedLessons.title: Server Actions and forms
advancedLessons.goal: Handle form submissions on the server without writing an API route.
body: A **Server Action** is an async function marked `"use server"`. Pass it to `<form action={fn}>` and it runs on the server with the form's `FormData`.
**Always validate** inside the action (Zod is ideal). It's a public endpoint: anyone can call it with any data.
`useActionState(action, initialState)` gives you the action's last return value (like validation errors) and a pending flag.
Forms with Server Actions work **before JavaScript loads** (progressive enhancement).

lessons.title: Variables, types and print
lessons.goal: Write and run your first Python script.
body: Python is known for being readable. There are no semicolons or curly braces: **indentation** (4 spaces) shows where blocks begin and end.
Run a script with `python3 hello.py`, or type `python3` to get an interactive prompt.
Types: `str`, `int`, `float`, `bool` (`True`/`False` are capitalized) and `None`. Python works out the type from the value.
**f-strings** put values inside text: `f"Hi {name}"`.

example.code:
name = "Ada"
age = 36
height = 1.68
is_student = True

print(f"{name} is {age} years old")
print(type(age).__name__, type(height).__name__, type(is_student).__name__)
print(age + 4, age / 5, age // 5)
print("Py" * 3)

Ada is 36 years old
int float bool
40 7.2 7
PyPyPy

`for item in collection:` loops over anything iterable. `range(5)` gives 0 to 4.
`while` repeats as long as a condition is true. Make sure it eventually becomes false!
Define functions with `def`. Use `and`, `or`, `not` (words, not symbols).
