lessons.title: Lists and dictionaries
lessons.goal: Store groups of data in lists and dicts, and loop over them.
body: A **list** is ordered and changeable: `nums = [3, 1, 2]`. Use `.append()`, `len()`, `sorted()` and slices like `nums[0:2]`.
A **dict** maps keys to values, like a JavaScript object: `user = {"name": "Ada", "age": 36}`.
`.get(key, default)` reads a key safely, without crashing when it's missing.
**List comprehensions** build a list in one line: `[n * 2 for n in nums if n > 1]`. That's Python's map plus filter.

example.code:
scores = [72, 95, 88, 61]
scores.append(99)
print(len(scores), max(scores), sorted(scores)[:3])

student = {"name": "Lee", "grade": 11}
student["club"] = "chess"
print(student["name"], student.get("email", "no email"))

for key, value in student.items():
    print(key, "=", value)

passed = [s for s in scores if s >= 70]
print(passed)

Lee no email

grade = 11

[72, 95, 88, 99]

intermediateLessons.title: Files, JSON and handling errors
intermediateLessons.goal: Read and write files and JSON safely, and handle what can go wrong.
body: `with open(path) as f:` opens a file and **always closes it**, even if an error happens.
`json.load(f)` reads JSON from a file, and `json.dump(data, f, indent=2)` writes it. `json.loads` and `json.dumps` work with strings.
`try / except SomeError / else / finally`. Catch **specific** errors (`FileNotFoundError`, `json.JSONDecodeError`, `ValueError`), never a bare `except:` that hides bugs.
`pathlib.Path` is the modern way to build file paths that work on any operating system.

intermediateLessons.title: Classes and objects
intermediateLessons.goal: Bundle data and behavior together with classes.
body: A **class** is a blueprint and an **object** is one thing built from it. `__init__` sets up a new object, and `self` is that object.
**Methods** are functions on the class. They always take `self` first.
`__repr__` controls how an object prints, which is great for debugging.
**Inheritance**: `class Ebook(Book):` gets everything from Book and can add or change methods. `super()` calls the parent's version.
`@dataclass` writes `__init__` and `__repr__` for you when a class is mostly data.

check.why: It removes boilerplate for data classes.

intermediateLessons.title: Modules, virtual environments and calling APIs
intermediateLessons.goal: Organize code into modules, isolate dependencies, and call a web API.
body: Any `.py` file is a **module**: `from utils import slugify`. Code under `if __name__ == "__main__":` only runs when the file is executed directly, not when it's imported.
A **virtual environment** keeps each project's packages separate: `python3 -m venv .venv`, then `source .venv/bin/activate` (Mac/Linux) or `.venv\Scripts\activate` (Windows).
Install packages with `pip install requests`, and record them with `pip freeze > requirements.txt`.
`requests.get(url, params=..., timeout=10)` calls an API. Call `raise_for_status()` to turn 4xx/5xx into an exception, and always set a **timeout**.

advancedLessons.title: Comprehensions and generators
advancedLessons.goal: Transform data concisely, and process huge data without loading it all into memory.
body: List, dict and set **comprehensions** build collections in one expression: `{name: len(name) for name in names}`.
A **generator** produces values one at a time with `yield`, pausing in between. It uses almost no memory, even for millions of items.
Generator **expressions** look like comprehensions in parentheses: `sum(x * x for x in range(10**6))`.
Chain generators into **pipelines**: read lines → parse → filter → total, processing one row at a time.

Generators chain: this one filters the stream from the first.

sum pulls the rest. The pipeline remembers where it stopped.
The list holds 100,000 numbers; the generator holds almost nothing.

advancedLessons.title: Decorators and type hints
advancedLessons.goal: Wrap functions with reusable behavior, and document types for tools and teammates.
body: A **decorator** is a function that takes a function and returns a new one that adds behavior: timing, logging, caching, auth checks. `@timer` above a def is shorthand for `fn = timer(fn)`.
Use `functools.wraps` inside so the wrapped function keeps its name and docstring.
The standard library has great ones: `@functools.cache`, `@dataclass`, `@property`, `@staticmethod`.
**Type hints** (`def total(prices: list[float]) -> float:`) aren't enforced when the code runs, but editors and **mypy** use them to catch bugs before running.

lessons.title: Tables, types and inserting data
lessons.goal: Create a table and insert rows.
body: A relational database stores data in **tables**: **rows** are records and **columns** are fields. Each column has a type.
Common PostgreSQL types: `INTEGER`, `TEXT`, `VARCHAR(n)`, `NUMERIC(10,2)` for money, `BOOLEAN`, `DATE`, and `TIMESTAMPTZ` for timestamps.
`SERIAL PRIMARY KEY` (or `INTEGER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY`) gives every row an automatic unique id.
Install PostgreSQL locally, or use a free hosted database such as Neon or Supabase. Open the `psql` shell to type commands.

lessons.title: SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY and LIMIT
lessons.goal: Read exactly the rows and columns you need.
body: `SELECT columns FROM table` reads data. `*` means every column, but naming the columns you need is clearer and faster.
`WHERE` filters rows: `=`, `<>` (not equal), `<`, `>`, `AND`, `OR`, `IN (...)`, `BETWEEN`, and `ILIKE '%dune%'` for case-insensitive text search.
`ORDER BY column DESC` sorts, and `LIMIT 5` returns at most 5 rows.
`COUNT(*)`, `AVG()`, `MIN()`, `MAX()` and `SUM()` summarize rows into one value.

lessons.title: UPDATE, DELETE and staying safe
lessons.goal: Change and remove rows without wiping the table.
body: `UPDATE table SET column = value WHERE ...` changes rows. `DELETE FROM table WHERE ...` removes them.
**Always write the WHERE first.** Without it, UPDATE changes every row and DELETE empties the table.
Run the same WHERE as a `SELECT` first to see which rows you're about to change.
`RETURNING *` shows you the rows that changed.

example.setup:
CREATE TABLE books (id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT, price NUMERIC(6,2), in_stock BOOLEAN DEFAULT true);

intermediateLessons.title: Primary keys, foreign keys and constraints
intermediateLessons.goal: Connect tables with foreign keys, and let the database enforce your rules.
body: A **foreign key** column stores another table's primary key, which links the rows: `author_id INTEGER REFERENCES authors(id)`.
The database then **refuses** bad data: you can't add a book for an author that doesn't exist.
`ON DELETE CASCADE` deletes child rows with their parent. `ON DELETE SET NULL` keeps them but clears the link.
Constraints are rules the database enforces for you: `NOT NULL`, `UNIQUE`, `CHECK (price >= 0)`. Data stays valid even if your app has a bug.

intermediateLessons.title: JOINs: combining tables
intermediateLessons.goal: Read data from several tables at once with INNER and LEFT JOIN.
body: `JOIN ... ON` matches rows across tables: `FROM books JOIN authors ON books.author_id = authors.id`.
**INNER JOIN** (or plain JOIN) keeps only rows that match on both sides.
**LEFT JOIN** keeps **every** row from the left table, filling in NULL when there's no match. Use it for "authors and their books, including authors with none".
Short **aliases** (`books b`, `authors a`) keep queries readable.

example.code:

FROM books b
JOIN authors a ON a.id = b.author_id
ORDER BY b.title;

SELECT a.name, b.title
FROM authors a
LEFT JOIN books b ON b.author_id = a.id
ORDER BY a.name, b.title;

intermediateLessons.title: GROUP BY, HAVING, and querying from Node
intermediateLessons.goal: Summarize data per group, and run safe parameterized queries from Node.js.
body: `GROUP BY` collapses rows into groups, and aggregates (`COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`) run per group.
`WHERE` filters rows **before** grouping. `HAVING` filters groups **after**: `HAVING COUNT(*) > 1`.
From Node, use the `pg` package with a connection **Pool**.
**Always use parameters** (`$1`, `$2`) for values. Never build SQL by joining strings with user input: that's **SQL injection**, one of the most common security holes.

example.setup:
CREATE TABLE orders (id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, customer TEXT, total NUMERIC(8,2));
INSERT INTO orders (customer, total) VALUES ('ana', 20), ('ana', 35), ('bo', 12), ('cy', 50), ('cy', 5), ('cy', 10);

demo.say: One row per customer, with a count and a total.
HAVING filters groups: only repeat customers.
Biggest spenders first.
A Pool reuses connections. The URL comes from an environment variable.
$1 and $2 are placeholders. pg sends the values separately, so input can never change the SQL.

practice.task: Find each customer's average order, only for orders over $8, showing customers whose average is above 20.
practice.hint: WHERE total > 8, GROUP BY customer, HAVING AVG(total) > 20.

solution.setup: CREATE TABLE orders (customer TEXT, total NUMERIC(8,2)); INSERT INTO orders VALUES ('ana', 20), ('ana', 35), ('bo', 12), ('cy', 50), ('cy', 5), ('cy', 10);
solution.code:
SELECT customer, ROUND(AVG(total), 2) AS avg_order
FROM orders
WHERE total > 8
GROUP BY customer
HAVING AVG(total) > 20
ORDER BY customer;

check.q: WHERE vs HAVING?
options: WHERE filters rows before grouping, HAVING filters groups after
check.why: HAVING can use aggregates like COUNT(*).

check.q: How do you prevent SQL injection?
check.why: Parameters are never parsed as SQL.

advancedLessons.title: Indexes and EXPLAIN
advancedLessons.goal: Make slow queries fast with indexes, and read a query plan.
body: Without an index, Postgres reads **every row** to find matches (a **Seq Scan**). An index is a sorted lookup structure, like a book's index, that jumps straight to matching rows.
`EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT ...` shows the plan Postgres chose and the real time each step took.
Index the columns you **filter, join and sort** on often, such as foreign keys and email lookups. Primary keys and UNIQUE columns are indexed automatically.
Indexes aren't free: they use space and slow down writes slightly. Don't index everything.

demo.say: 50,000 fake events for 5,000 users. ANALYZE updates the statistics the planner uses.
No index: Postgres must read every row.
Add an index on the column we filter by.
Now it looks up the matching rows directly.
demo.out:
Bitmap Heap Scan on events
  -> Bitmap Index Scan on events_user_id_idx

practice.task: Which index helps `SELECT * FROM events WHERE user_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20`?
practice.hint: One index can cover both the filter and the sort.

solution.setup: CREATE TABLE events (id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, user_id INTEGER, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now());
solution.code: CREATE INDEX events_user_recent_idx ON events (user_id, created_at DESC);

check.q: What does a Seq Scan mean?
check.why: A sequential scan reads the whole table.

check.q: A cost of adding indexes?
options: Extra storage and slightly slower writes
check.why: Every insert or update must also update the index.

advancedLessons.title: Transactions
advancedLessons.goal: Group changes so they all succeed or all fail together.
body: A **transaction** wraps several statements: `BEGIN; ... COMMIT;`. If anything goes wrong, `ROLLBACK` undoes everything since BEGIN.
Classic example: a transfer must take money from one account **and** add it to another. Half a transfer is a disaster.
Postgres guarantees **ACID**: Atomic (all or nothing), Consistent (constraints hold), Isolated (others don't see half-done work), Durable (committed means saved).
In Node with `pg`, take one client from the pool, run BEGIN, your queries and COMMIT on that **same client**, and ROLLBACK in `catch`.

demo.say: A CHECK constraint: balances can never go negative.
Both updates commit together. Ana has 70 and Bo has 50.
Start a transfer that's too big...
...but Ana only has 70. (Taking 500 would also break the CHECK and abort the transaction.)
Roll back: Bo's +500 is undone as if it never happened.
Only the first transfer happened.

practice.task: Write the Node.js version of a transfer with pg, using one client and ROLLBACK on error.
practice.hint: `const client = await pool.connect()` … `finally { client.release() }`

check.q: What does ROLLBACK do?
check.why: All or nothing.

check.q: Why use one client for the whole transaction?
options: A transaction belongs to one connection
check.why: Queries on other pool connections aren't in the transaction.

advancedLessons.title: Schema design, normalization and migrations
advancedLessons.goal: Design tables that avoid duplicate data, and change schemas safely over time.
body: **Normalization** means storing each fact once. If an author's name is copied into every book row, renaming them means updating many rows, and missing one causes contradictions.
**Many-to-many** relationships (books ↔ tags) need a **join table** with two foreign keys and a composite primary key.
**Denormalize on purpose** only when reads are slow and measured, and keep the copy in sync.

**Migrations** are versioned SQL files (`001_create_books.sql`, `002_add_tags.sql`) applied in order, checked into git. Tools: node-pg-migrate, Prisma Migrate, Drizzle Kit. Never edit a migration that has already run in production; add a new one.

demo.say: Migration 1: the author's name is stored once; books point to it.
Migration 2 adds tags. A book has many tags, and a tag has many books: a join table.
The composite primary key stops the same tag being added to a book twice.
Kindred is sci-fi and classic; Dawn is sci-fi.
Count books per tag through the join table.

practice.task: A `students` table has columns course1, course2, course3. What's wrong, and what's the better design?
practice.hint: What happens with a fourth course?

solution.output:
CREATE TABLE
CREATE TABLE
CREATE TABLE

check.q: Many-to-many needs…
options: Two foreign keys in one table
check.why: A join table holds one row per pair.

check.q: A migration already ran in production and has a bug. You should…
options: Write a new migration that fixes it
check.why: Migrations are history; add, don't rewrite.

modules.name: Express.js
modules.blurb: Build a Node.js web server and API, with morgan for request logging.

lessons.title: Your first Express server
lessons.goal: Start a Node server and respond to routes.
body: **Express** is a small framework for building web servers with Node.js. Set up with `npm init -y`, then `npm install express`.
Add `"type": "module"` to package.json to use `import` syntax.
A **route** is a method plus a path plus a handler: `app.get("/", (req, res) => ...)`. `req` is the incoming request and `res` is your response.
`res.send()` sends text or HTML, `res.json()` sends JSON, and `res.status(404)` sets the status code.
`app.listen(3000)` starts the server. Visit http://localhost:3000.

demo.say: Import Express and create the app.
Use the PORT environment variable in production, or 3000 locally.
GET / sends back HTML.
GET /api/status sends JSON, the usual format for APIs.
Start listening, and log the address.

practice.task: Add GET /api/hello that returns { message: "Hello" }, and a catch-all at the end that returns a 404 JSON error.
practice.hint: Put `app.use((req, res) => res.status(404).json({ error: "Not found" }))` after all your routes.

check.q: Which sends JSON?
check.why: res.json serializes the object and sets the JSON content type.

check.q: Where does a catch-all 404 handler go?
check.why: Express runs things in order, so the fallback goes last.

lessons.title: Route params, query strings and JSON bodies
lessons.goal: Read input from req.params, req.query and req.body.
body: **Route params** are parts of the path: `/api/books/:id` puts the id in `req.params.id`.
**Query strings** come after `?`: `/api/books?author=Butler` puts it in `req.query.author`.
**JSON bodies** (from POST and PUT) need `app.use(express.json())`, then you read them from `req.body`.
Everything arrives as **text**, so convert numbers with `Number()` and **validate** before trusting it.

demo.say: Without this line, req.body is undefined.
GET /api/books?author=Herbert filters the list by the query string.
`:id` becomes req.params.id, which is a string, so convert it with Number().
Return early with a 404 when nothing matches.
Read the JSON body and validate it, sending 400 for bad input.
Create the book and answer 201 Created.

practice.task: Add DELETE /api/books/:id that removes the book and returns 204 (no content), or 404 if it doesn't exist.
practice.hint: Use findIndex and splice, then `res.status(204).end()`.

check.q: In /users/:id, where is the id?
check.why: Path segments with a colon land in req.params.

check.q: Status for 'you sent invalid data'?
check.why: 400 Bad Request means the client's input was wrong.

lessons.title: Middleware and logging with morgan
lessons.goal: Understand middleware order and log every request with morgan.
body: **Middleware** is a function that runs on requests **before** your routes: `(req, res, next) => { ...; next(); }`. Calling `next()` passes the request along. Forget it and the request hangs.
`app.use()` adds middleware. **Order matters**: Express runs everything top to bottom.
**morgan** is middleware that logs every request: method, path, status and time. Install with `npm install morgan`.
Use `morgan("dev")` locally for short colored logs, and `morgan("combined")` in production for the standard log format.

demo.say: Import morgan after installing it.
First middleware: log every request.
Second: parse JSON bodies.
Your own middleware: add data to req, then call next().
The route can read what the middleware added.

practice.task: Write middleware that rejects any request without the header `x-api-key: secret123` with a 401.
practice.hint: `req.get("x-api-key")` reads a header. Return before calling next().

check.q: What happens if middleware never calls next() or responds?
check.why: The request never moves on and never gets a response.

check.q: What does morgan do?
check.why: morgan is a request logger.

project.title: Notes REST API
project.brief: An Express API for notes (GET all, GET one, POST, DELETE) stored in an array, with morgan logging, JSON validation and proper status codes. Test it with a tool like Postman or Thunder Client.
steps: npm init, express, morgan, "type": "module"
GET /api/notes and GET /api/notes/:id
POST with validation (400 on a missing title)
DELETE with 204 and 404
A 404 catch-all and morgan('dev')
test: POST with no title gives 400
GET /api/notes/999 gives 404
Every request appears in the morgan log

intermediateLessons.title: A full CRUD API with Express Router
intermediateLessons.goal: Organize routes into a router and implement create, read, update and delete.
body: **CRUD** maps onto HTTP: Create = `POST /notes`, Read = `GET /notes` and `GET /notes/:id`, Update = `PATCH /notes/:id` (or PUT to replace), Delete = `DELETE /notes/:id`.
`express.Router()` groups related routes in their own file. Mount it with `app.use("/api/notes", notesRouter)`, and the paths inside become relative.
Use the right status codes: 201 Created (with the new item), 204 No Content after a delete, 404 when the id doesn't exist, 400 for bad input.
PATCH should only change the fields that were sent.

demo.say: A router is a mini-app for one resource.
GET /api/notes: the list.
GET one, or a 404.
POST validates, creates and answers 201 with the new note.
PATCH only touches the fields that were sent.
DELETE answers 204 with an empty body.
Mounted at /api/notes, so the router's "/" means /api/notes.

practice.task: Add `GET /api/notes?done=true` filtering to the list route.
practice.hint: Read req.query.done, which is a string, so compare to "true".

check.q: Status after a successful DELETE with no body?
check.why: 204 No Content.

check.q: PATCH vs PUT?
options: PATCH changes some fields; PUT replaces the whole resource
check.why: PATCH is a partial update.

intermediateLessons.title: Validation and error-handling middleware
intermediateLessons.goal: Validate input in one place and send every error through one handler.
body: Write **validation middleware** that checks `req.body` and either calls `next()` or answers 400 with the problems listed.
An **error-handling middleware** has **four** parameters: `(err, req, res, next)`. Register it **last**. Any route that throws or calls `next(err)` ends up there.
Express 5 also catches errors from `async` route handlers automatically.
Never send stack traces or database messages to users. Log the details on the server and send a short, safe message.

demo.say: An error type that carries an HTTP status.
Reusable validation: list the required fields, get a middleware back.
Validation runs before the handler. Missing fields never reach it.
Throwing inside an async handler is caught by Express 5.
Four parameters make this the error handler. Unknown errors are logged and hidden.

practice.task: Extend requireFields into `validate(schema)` where schema maps field names to a check function, e.g. `{ price: (v) => v >= 0 }`.
practice.hint: Collect the fields whose check fails.

check.q: How does Express recognize error-handling middleware?
check.why: (err, req, res, next).

check.q: What should a 500 response contain?
check.why: Details go in your logs, not to the user.

intermediateLessons.title: Express + PostgreSQL, CORS and environment variables
intermediateLessons.goal: Store API data in Postgres, configure CORS, and keep settings in .env.
body: Create one `pg.Pool` for the whole app and query it with parameters (`$1`).
Put settings in a `.env` file (`DATABASE_URL`, `PORT`, `CLIENT_URL`) and load them with `node --env-file=.env server.js` (built into Node 20+) or the `dotenv` package. Keep `.env` out of git.
**CORS:** browsers block a page on one origin from reading responses from another, unless the server allows it. Use the `cors` middleware and allow **only your frontend's origin**, not `*`.
`RETURNING *` gives back the inserted or updated row in the same query.

demo.say: One pool, shared by every request. The URL comes from .env.
Only your frontend (e.g. http://localhost:5173) may call this API from a browser.
Read from the database. rows is an array of plain objects.
$1 is a parameter, so the title can never inject SQL. RETURNING gives back the new row.
Settings come from the environment, so nothing secret lives in the code.

practice.task: Write the .env file and the CREATE TABLE statement this API needs.
practice.hint: notes: id, title, done with a default.

solution.code:
CREATE TABLE notes (
  id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  title TEXT NOT NULL,
  done BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT false
);
-- .env
-- DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:pass@localhost:5432/notes
-- CLIENT_URL=http://localhost:5173
-- PORT=3000

check.q: What does CORS control?
options: Which servers your API can call
Which browser origins may read your API's responses
check.why: CORS is a browser rule the server opts into.

check.q: Should origin be '*' for an API with logins?
options: No, allow only your own frontend
check.why: Allow the narrowest set of origins.

advancedLessons.title: Authentication: password hashing and JWTs
advancedLessons.goal: Store passwords safely and issue tokens that prove who a user is.
body: **Never store passwords.** Store a slow, salted **hash** (bcrypt or argon2). At login, hash the attempt and compare. Even you can't see users' passwords.
After login the server needs to remember the user. Two common ways: a **session** (a random id in a cookie, with the data on the server) or a **JWT** (a signed token holding the user id).
A JWT is **signed, not encrypted**: anyone can read its contents, but nobody can change them without the secret. Never put secrets inside one, and keep tokens short-lived.
Send tokens in an `httpOnly`, `secure`, `sameSite` cookie, so JavaScript on the page (and any XSS attack) can't read them.

example.output:
true 60
true
false
user_42 member
member
rejected: invalid signature

demo.say: The signing secret comes from the environment, never from git.
Hash with cost 12. The result includes its own salt.
Login: compare the attempt to the stored hash.
Sign a short-lived token with the user id, then verify it on later requests.
Anyone can decode the payload. Signed is not secret!
Tampering breaks the signature.
Deliver it in a cookie that page JavaScript can't read.

practice.task: Write `requireAuth` Express middleware that reads the token cookie, verifies it, puts the payload on `req.user`, and answers 401 otherwise.
practice.hint: Use cookie-parser for req.cookies, and jwt.verify in try/catch.

check.q: How should passwords be stored?
options: Plain text in a private table
check.why: Hashes can't be reversed; slowness defeats guessing.

check.q: Can a user read the contents of their JWT?
check.why: Signing prevents changes, not reading.

advancedLessons.title: Security headers, rate limiting and input limits
advancedLessons.goal: Harden an Express API against the most common attacks.
body: **helmet** sets a batch of security headers in one line: no sniffing content types, no framing your site (clickjacking), strict HTTPS, and more.
**Rate limiting** (`express-rate-limit`) caps requests per IP, which slows down password guessing and scraping. Use a strict limit on `/login`.
**Limit body size**: `express.json({ limit: "10kb" })` stops someone sending a 1GB request.
Other essentials: parameterized SQL (no injection), validate every input, never leak stack traces, keep dependencies updated (`npm audit`), and serve over HTTPS.

demo.say: Don't advertise that you're running Express.
helmet adds headers like X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options and Strict-Transport-Security.
Bodies over 10kb are rejected with 413.
At most 100 API requests per minute per IP, with RateLimit headers telling clients where they stand.
Login gets a much stricter limit: 5 tries per 15 minutes.
The same message whether the email or the password was wrong, so attackers can't discover which emails exist.
A normal route still works, now with helmet's headers on every response.

practice.task: Run `npm audit` on one of your projects. What do the severity levels mean, and what does `npm audit fix` do?
practice.hint: Look at the advisory links in the output.

solution.code:
Levels: low, moderate, high, critical (how bad the vulnerability is if it's reachable).
npm audit fix upgrades to patched versions within your allowed ranges.
npm audit fix --force may install breaking major versions, so run your tests afterwards.
Check whether the vulnerable code is actually used: many dev-only advisories don't affect production.

check.q: Why give /login its own stricter rate limit?
check.why: Brute-force attacks target login.

check.q: Why the same error for 'wrong email' and 'wrong password'?
options: So attackers can't learn which emails have accounts
check.why: Different messages leak account existence.

advancedLessons.title: Production readiness: logs, health checks and shutdown
advancedLessons.goal: Run a Node API the way production platforms expect.
body: Log **structured JSON** (one object per line, with a level, message and request id) so you can search logs. morgan's `combined` format or a logger like pino works well.
Add a `GET /healthz` route that returns 200 when the app is ready. Hosting platforms and load balancers poll it.
**Graceful shutdown:** on `SIGTERM` (sent when a platform redeploys), stop accepting new connections, finish the requests in flight, close the database pool, then exit.
Read **all** config from environment variables, crash early with a clear message if one is missing, and run with `NODE_ENV=production`.

demo.say: Every request gets an id, which is also sent back in a header for support tickets.
When the response finishes, log one JSON line.
A health check for the platform to poll.
On SIGTERM: stop taking new requests, let current ones finish, then exit.
Don't hang forever: force-exit after 10 seconds. unref() keeps this timer from holding the process open.

practice.task: Write a `requireEnv(name)` helper that returns process.env[name] or throws a clear error at startup.
practice.hint: Call it at the top of server.js for every required variable.

check.q: What's SIGTERM?
options: The polite 'please shut down' signal platforms send before stopping your app
check.why: Handle it to finish in-flight requests.

check.q: Why structured JSON logs?
options: They can be searched and filtered by field
check.why: Log tools index the fields.

modules.name: Firebase
modules.blurb: Google's back end for auth, a database and hosting, without running a server.

docs.label: Firebase: Add to a web app

lessons.title: What Firebase is, and setup
lessons.goal: Create a Firebase project and connect a web app.
body: **Firebase** is Google's set of back-end services: **Authentication** (sign-in), **Firestore** (a NoSQL database), **Hosting**, **Storage** and more. You get a back end without writing a server.
Steps: create a project at console.firebase.google.com, add a **Web app**, copy the config object, then run `npm install firebase`.
The web config (apiKey and the rest) is **not a secret**: it identifies your project. Your data is protected by **Security Rules**, so set them before you go live.
Keep the config in environment variables anyway, so you can switch between projects.

demo.say: The modular SDK: import only what you use.
The config comes from .env (in Next.js, use process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_...).
Initialize once, in a single file.
Export auth and db so every other file imports from here.

practice.task: Create a Firebase project, enable Email/Password sign-in, create a Firestore database in test mode, and put your config in a .env file.

VITE_FB_AUTH_DOMAIN=yourapp.firebaseapp.com

check.q: What actually protects Firestore data?
check.why: Security Rules decide who can read and write.

check.q: How many times should you call initializeApp?
check.why: Initialize once and export the instances.

lessons.title: Email/password authentication
lessons.goal: Sign users up, in and out, and react to auth changes.
body: `createUserWithEmailAndPassword(auth, email, password)` signs up, and `signInWithEmailAndPassword` signs in. Both return a Promise and throw on failure.
Errors have a `code` like `auth/invalid-credential` or `auth/email-already-in-use`. Turn these into friendly messages.
`onAuthStateChanged(auth, callback)` runs whenever someone signs in or out, **including on page load**. Use it to know who's logged in.
`signOut(auth)` logs the user out.

demo.say: Import the functions you need, plus your shared auth instance.
Create the account. The new user comes back on success.
Map Firebase error codes to messages people understand.
Sign in and sign out are one-liners.
This listener fires on load and on every change, so it's the one source of truth for who's logged in.

practice.task: Build a sign-in form that shows the error message under the form instead of an alert.
practice.hint: Catch the error and set `errorEl.textContent`. Add `role="alert"` so screen readers announce it.

check.q: When does onAuthStateChanged fire?
options: On load and on every sign-in or sign-out
check.why: It also reports the restored session on page load.

check.q: Where is the error type?
check.why: Firebase errors carry a string code.

lessons.title: Firestore: add and read documents
lessons.goal: Write documents to a collection and read them back.
body: Firestore stores **documents** (JSON-like objects) inside **collections**. Each document has an id.
`addDoc(collection(db, "notes"), data)` adds a document with an automatic id. `setDoc(doc(db, "users", uid), data)` writes one with an id you choose.
`getDocs(collection(...))` reads all the documents once. `query()` with `where()` and `orderBy()` filters them.
Use `serverTimestamp()` for created-at times, so every user's clock doesn't matter.

demo.say: Add a note to the notes collection, tagged with the signed-in user's id.
The server sets the time.
Build a query: only my notes, newest first.
Run it, then combine each document's id with its data.

practice.task: Write `deleteNote(id)` using `deleteDoc(doc(db, "notes", id))`.
practice.hint: Import deleteDoc and doc from firebase/firestore.

check.q: addDoc vs setDoc?
options: addDoc auto-generates the id; setDoc uses yours
check.why: setDoc writes to a specific document id.

check.q: Why serverTimestamp()?
check.why: Users' device clocks can be wrong.

project.title: Private notes app
project.brief: Sign up and log in with email, add and delete notes, and see only your own notes. Add a Firestore rule so nobody can read anyone else's notes.
steps: Firebase project, auth and Firestore
A sign-up / log-in form with friendly errors
Show the notes list only when signed in (onAuthStateChanged)
Add and delete notes

A wrong password shows a message, not a crash

intermediateLessons.title: Google sign-in and auth state in React
intermediateLessons.goal: Add Google sign-in and share the signed-in user across a React app.
body: Enable Google in Firebase Console → Authentication → Sign-in method. Then `signInWithPopup(auth, new GoogleAuthProvider())`.
Wrap `onAuthStateChanged` in a React context so every component knows the user. Track a `loading` flag too: on page load Firebase needs a moment to restore the session.
Until `loading` is false, show a skeleton, not the logged-out screen. Otherwise signed-in users see a flash of the sign-in page.
Remember: hiding a page in React is only **UX**. Protect the data itself with Security Rules.

demo.say: The user, plus a loading flag that starts true.
onAuthStateChanged returns its unsubscribe function, which doubles as the effect's cleanup.
Google sign-in in one line.
The usual guard hook.
While Firebase restores the session, show a neutral placeholder.
Then the right button for the real state.

practice.task: Write a `RequireAuth` component that shows its children only when signed in, a sign-in button when not, and nothing while loading.
practice.hint: Read useAuth() and branch on loading, then user.

check.q: Why track loading separately from user?
options: user is null both before restore and when logged out
check.why: Without it, signed-in users briefly see the logged-out UI.

check.q: Does hiding a page in React protect the data?
check.why: Client-side checks are UX only.

intermediateLessons.title: Firestore queries and real-time listeners
intermediateLessons.goal: Filter, sort and limit queries, and keep a list updated live with onSnapshot.
body: `query(collection(db, "notes"), where("owner", "==", uid), orderBy("createdAt", "desc"), limit(20))`.
Combining `where` on one field with `orderBy` on another needs a **composite index**. Firestore's error message includes a link that creates it for you.
`onSnapshot(q, callback)` calls you now **and on every change**, from any device. It returns an unsubscribe function: call it in your effect's cleanup.
Each document read counts toward your quota, so always `limit()` lists.

demo.say: A custom hook: any component can get the user's live notes.
No user yet? Don't query.
My notes, newest first, at most 20.
Runs now and every time a matching note changes, even from another device.
Errors (missing index, denied by rules) are surfaced, not swallowed.

practice.task: Change the hook so it also returns a `loading` boolean that's true until the first snapshot arrives.
practice.hint: Start loading at true, and set it false in both callbacks.

check.q: What does onSnapshot return?
check.why: Call it to stop listening.

check.q: where on owner + orderBy on createdAt needs…
check.why: Firestore needs an index for that combination.

intermediateLessons.title: Security Rules basics
intermediateLessons.goal: Write Firestore rules so users can only read and write their own data.
body: Security Rules run on Google's servers for **every** read and write. They're the real protection, because anyone can call Firestore directly with your public config.
`request.auth` is the signed-in user (null if not signed in). `resource.data` is the document **as it is now**, and `request.resource.data` is the document **as it would be** after the write.
Start from **deny everything**, then open exactly what each collection needs.
Test rules in the Rules Playground in the console, or with the Firebase emulator (Advanced).

demo.say: Rules for each document in notes.
Read or delete only your own notes: compare the user id to the stored owner.
Create only as yourself, with text that's a string of at most 500 characters.
Update your own notes, and you can't hand them to someone else.
Everything else is denied.

practice.task: Write a rule for a `profiles/{uid}` collection: anyone signed in can read profiles, but only the owner (where uid matches) can write theirs.
practice.hint: Compare `request.auth.uid == uid` using the wildcard.

check.q: request.resource.data is…
options: The document as it would be after the write
check.why: resource.data is now; request.resource.data is after.

check.q: A good starting point for rules is…
options: Deny everything, then open what's needed
check.why: Default-deny is safest.

advancedLessons.title: Data modeling in Firestore
advancedLessons.goal: Shape Firestore data around your queries, not around tables.
body: Firestore has **no joins**. Design documents around the screens that read them: ask "what does this page need in one query?"
**Denormalize** small, rarely-changing data: store the author's name on each post, so a feed doesn't need a second read per post.
**Subcollections** (`posts/{postId}/comments`) are good for unbounded lists that belong to one parent. A document has a 1MB limit, so never put a growing list in an array field.
Use **counters** (updated with `increment()` or a Cloud Function) instead of counting thousands of documents, and **batched writes** to update several documents atomically.

demo.say: The plan: authorName is copied onto posts and comments so feeds need one read. commentCount avoids counting.
A batch, and a new comment document in the post's subcollection.
Denormalized: the author's name is stored with the comment.
increment() updates the counter safely, even with many users at once.
Both writes succeed or neither does.
Read the 20 newest comments for one post.

practice.task: A user changes their display name. What has to happen with the denormalized authorName copies, and where should that code run?
practice.hint: Many documents, triggered by one change.

solution.code:
Every post and comment with that authorId needs its authorName updated.
Run it in a Cloud Function triggered when users/{uid} changes, using batched writes (max 500 per batch).
Or decide that old posts keep the old name, which is often fine and much cheaper.
This trade-off is the cost of denormalizing.

check.q: Where should an unbounded list of comments go?
options: An array field on the post
check.why: Documents max out at 1MB; subcollections don't.

check.q: Why store authorName on each post?
options: So a feed can render without an extra read per post
check.why: Firestore has no joins; denormalize for reads.

advancedLessons.title: Cloud Functions
advancedLessons.goal: Run trusted server code on Firebase: triggers, callable functions and scheduled jobs.
body: **Cloud Functions** run your Node code on Google's servers. Use them for anything the client must not be trusted with: payments, sending email, keeping counters, admin actions.
**Triggers** run when data changes: `onDocumentCreated("posts/{id}/comments/{cid}", ...)`.
**Callable functions** (`onCall`) are called from your app like an API, and arrive with the user's auth already verified.

Functions use the **Admin SDK**, which ignores Security Rules, so check permissions yourself. Store secrets with `defineSecret`, never in code. Functions require the pay-as-you-go plan (with a generous free tier).

demo.say: The Admin SDK: full access, ignoring Security Rules.
A trigger keeps the counter correct, so clients can't fake it.
Callable: auth arrives verified. Reject anonymous calls.
Admin access means YOU must check ownership.
A scheduled job: delete drafts untouched for 30 days, 500 at a time.

practice.task: Call deletePost from a React button.
practice.hint: httpsCallable(getFunctions(), "deletePost")

check.q: Do Security Rules apply to the Admin SDK?
options: No, so check permissions in your function
check.why: Admin access bypasses rules.

check.q: Good job for a Cloud Function?
options: Charging a card or sending email
check.why: Trusted work that needs secrets.

advancedLessons.title: The Emulator Suite and testing Security Rules
advancedLessons.goal: Develop against local Firebase emulators and prove your rules with tests.
body: The **Emulator Suite** runs Auth, Firestore, Functions and Storage on your machine: `firebase emulators:start`. There's no risk to real data and no cost, and you can reset everything.
Point your app at them in development with `connectFirestoreEmulator(db, "127.0.0.1", 8080)` and `connectAuthEmulator`.
**Test your Security Rules** with `@firebase/rules-unit-testing`: create fake signed-in users and assert what each can and can't do. Rules are security code, so they deserve tests.
Run these tests in CI so a rule change can never silently open up your data.

demo.say: Load your real rules file into the local emulator. "demo-" projects never touch the cloud.
Every test starts with an empty database.
A fake signed-in user, Ana, may create her own note.
She may NOT create a note owned by Bo.
Seed Bo's note with rules off, then prove Ana can't read it.

practice.task: Add a test proving a signed-OUT visitor can't read any note.
practice.hint: env.unauthenticatedContext()

check.q: Why use the emulators in development?
options: No risk to real data, no cost, easy reset
check.why: Safe, free and repeatable.

check.q: Rules tests should cover…
options: What each kind of user can AND can't do
check.why: Security is about what's denied.

lessons.title: Why test, and the shape of a test
lessons.goal: Know what a unit test is and the Arrange–Act–Assert pattern.
body: A **test** is code that runs your code and checks the result. When you change something later, the tests tell you right away if you broke it.
A **unit test** checks one small piece, like a single function, in isolation. Most of your tests should be unit tests: they're fast and precise.
Every test has three parts: **Arrange** (set up the input), **Act** (run the code), **Assert** (check the result).
Test **behavior**, not implementation: check what the function returns or what the user sees, not how it works inside. Then you can rewrite the inside without rewriting the tests.
Good first targets: pure functions (calculations, formatting, validation). They're the easiest to test.

demo.say: The function we want to prove works.
A tiny test runner: run fn, print ✓ if nothing throws, ✗ if something does.
Arrange: set up the input.
Act: call the code.
Assert: throw if the result is wrong.
Test the error case too. Edge cases are where bugs hide.

practice.task: List four test cases for a function `isValidUsername(name)` that requires 3–15 characters, letters and numbers only.
practice.hint: Cover a normal case, both length limits, and a bad character.

solution.code:
"sam99" → true (normal)
"ab" → false (too short)
"a" repeated 16 times → false (too long)
"sam!" → false (bad character)
Bonus: "abc" → true (exactly the minimum)

check.q: The three parts of a test, in order?
check.why: Arrange the inputs, Act by calling the code, Assert on the result.

check.q: Which is easiest to unit test?
options: A function that calls an API
check.why: Pure functions: same input, same output, no setup.

lessons.title: Your first tests with Vitest
lessons.goal: Install Vitest and write tests with describe, it and expect.
body: **Vitest** is a fast test runner that works like **Jest** (same `describe`, `it`, `expect`), so learning one teaches you both. Install with `npm install -D vitest` and add `"test": "vitest"` to your package.json scripts.
Name test files `something.test.js`, next to the code they test.
`expect(value)` has **matchers**: `.toBe()` for exact primitives, `.toEqual()` for objects and arrays (it compares contents), `.toThrow()`, `.toContain()`, `.toBeTruthy()`.
`npm test` re-runs your tests every time you save a file.

demo.say: Import the test functions.
Normally you'd import this from cart.js. It's inline here to keep it short.
describe groups the related tests.
Each `it` is one behavior. Start with the edge case: an empty cart.
The normal case: 5×2 + 3×1 = 13.
toEqual compares an object's contents. toBe would compare identity.

practice.task: Write Vitest tests for your `calcSplit(bill, tipPct, people)` from the JavaScript project: a normal split, 0% tip, and people = 0 throwing an error.
practice.hint: `expect(() => calcSplit(100, 10, 0)).toThrow()`. Wrap the call in a function!

check.q: Compare two arrays' contents with…
check.why: toBe checks identity, so two different arrays fail even with the same items.

check.q: How do you test that a function throws?
check.why: Wrap it, so expect can catch the throw itself.

lessons.title: Testing React components
lessons.goal: Render a component and test it the way a user would use it.
body: **React Testing Library** (RTL) renders a component in a fake browser (jsdom) and lets you find things the way a user does: by role, label or text.
Install: `npm install -D @testing-library/react @testing-library/user-event @testing-library/jest-dom jsdom`, and set `test: { environment: "jsdom" }` in vite.config.

Prefer queries in this order: `getByRole` (button, heading, textbox), then `getByLabelText`, then `getByText`. If you can't find an element by role, real users of screen readers probably can't either.
Use `userEvent` to click and type. It behaves like a real user, including focus and key presses.

demo.say: render and screen come from RTL, user events from user-event, and extra matchers from jest-dom.
Arrange: set up a user and render the component.
Assert the starting state, which is what the user sees.
Act: click the button whose accessible name is "+".
Assert the result.
Test the edge case from the React lesson's practice.

practice.task: Test your to-do list: typing "Buy milk" and pressing Enter shows "Buy milk" in the list.
practice.hint: `await user.type(screen.getByRole("textbox"), "Buy milk{Enter}")`

check.q: Which query should you try first?
check.why: Role queries match how users and assistive technology find elements.

check.q: Why test with user-event instead of calling functions directly?
check.why: You test what the user does and sees, not the internals.

lessons.title: Testing Python with pytest
lessons.goal: Write and run pytest tests with plain assert.
body: **pytest** is the standard Python test runner. Install with `pip install pytest`.
Name files `test_something.py` and functions `test_something()`. pytest finds them automatically.
Just use `assert`: `assert add(2, 3) == 5`. When it fails, pytest shows you both values.
`pytest.raises(ValueError)` checks that an error is raised. Run everything with `pytest` in the terminal.

demo.say: The function under test, with validation.
A test is just a function whose name starts with test_.
Test both sides of a boundary: off-by-one bugs live at 89/90.
pytest.raises passes only if the error happens.

practice.task: Write pytest tests for `check_guess(guess, secret)` from the Python project: higher, lower and correct.
practice.hint: Three small test functions, each with one assert.

check.q: How does pytest find tests?
options: By file and function names starting with test
check.why: Test discovery uses the test_ naming convention.

check.q: pytest checks values with…
check.why: pytest rewrites plain assert to show helpful failure messages.

project.title: Test your projects
project.brief: Go back and add tests to three earlier projects: the tip calculator (Vitest), the React to-do list (React Testing Library), and the number guessing game (pytest).
steps: Set up Vitest in the tip calculator
At least 4 tests for calcSplit, including edge cases
RTL tests: add, toggle and delete a to-do
pytest tests for check_guess
Break the code on purpose and watch a test fail
test: npm test and pytest both pass
Each project has at least one edge-case test
You saw every test fail at least once (proof it can catch bugs)

intermediateLessons.title: Testing async code and mocking fetch
intermediateLessons.goal: Test functions that call APIs, without hitting the real network.
body: Tests that call real APIs are slow and flaky. Replace `fetch` with a **mock** that returns what you choose.
`vi.fn()` makes a fake function that records how it was called. `vi.stubGlobal("fetch", mockFn)` swaps the global fetch for one test, and `vi.unstubAllGlobals()` restores it.
Use `async` tests and `await` the code. `await expect(promise).rejects.toThrow()` checks for failures.
Test the **unhappy paths** too: 404, network failure, empty results. That's where real bugs live.

demo.say: The code under test calls the real global fetch.
A helper that builds a fake Response with just the parts we use.
Put the real fetch back after each test.
Swap in a mock that answers 200 with a user.
Check the result, and that the right URL was requested.
The 404 path: getUser should throw a clear error.
A network failure (fetch itself rejects).

practice.task: Write a test proving `searchBooks("")` returns [] WITHOUT calling fetch at all.
practice.hint: Stub fetch with vi.fn(), then `expect(fetchMock).not.toHaveBeenCalled()`.

check.q: Why mock fetch in unit tests?
options: Real APIs make tests slow, flaky and dependent on the network
check.why: Mocks make tests fast and deterministic.

check.q: How do you test a rejected promise?
check.why: rejects unwraps the promise for the matcher.

intermediateLessons.title: Testing forms, user events and custom hooks
intermediateLessons.goal: Test a form the way a user fills it in, and test a custom hook on its own.
body: Find inputs by label: `getByLabelText("Email")`. If that fails, your form probably isn't accessible.
`await user.type(input, "ana@example.com")`, `await user.click(button)`, `await user.keyboard("{Enter}")` behave like a real person.
Pass mock callbacks (`const onDone = vi.fn()`) and assert on what they received.
`renderHook` from Testing Library runs a custom hook without a component. Wrap state changes in `act()`.

demo.say: A mock callback stands in for the parent.
Click submit with empty fields.
Errors are shown, the field is marked invalid, and nothing is submitted.
Type into fields found by their labels, just like a user.
The callback got exactly the form data.
renderHook tests a hook alone. act() wraps the state change.

practice.task: Test that pressing Enter in the email field submits the form.
practice.hint: `await user.type(emailInput, "ana@example.com{Enter}")`

check.q: getByLabelText fails to find your input. That suggests…
options: The input has no proper label
check.why: If tests can't find it by label, screen readers can't either.

check.q: What is renderHook for?
options: Testing a custom hook without writing a component
check.why: It runs the hook inside a tiny test component for you.

intermediateLessons.title: Coverage, and pytest fixtures and parametrize
intermediateLessons.goal: Read a coverage report sensibly, and remove repetition from Python tests.
body: **Coverage** reports which lines ran during your tests: `npx vitest run --coverage` or `pytest --cov`. Low coverage shows untested code. **High coverage doesn't prove the tests are good**: a test can run a line without checking its result.
Aim coverage at what matters: business logic, validation and edge cases. Don't chase 100% on simple glue code.
**Fixtures** in pytest provide setup for tests: a function decorated with `@pytest.fixture`, requested by naming it as a test parameter.
`@pytest.mark.parametrize` runs one test with many inputs. Each case is reported separately.

demo.say: A fixture: every test that asks for cart gets a fresh one with 2 ferns.
Request the fixture by naming it as a parameter.
One test, three cases. Each shows up separately in the results.
The test body runs once per row.
Parametrize the edge cases too.

practice.task: Parametrize a test for `is_leap(year)` with 2024 → True, 1900 → False, 2000 → True, 2023 → False.
practice.hint: `@pytest.mark.parametrize("year, expected", [...])`

check.q: 100% coverage means…
options: Every line ran during tests, not that results were checked
check.why: Coverage measures execution, not correctness.

check.q: How does a test get a pytest fixture?
check.why: pytest injects fixtures by parameter name.

advancedLessons.title: Integration tests for APIs with supertest
advancedLessons.goal: Test real HTTP routes, status codes and validation without starting a server.
body: **Integration tests** exercise several parts together, here the routing, middleware, validation and handler, through real HTTP requests.
**supertest** sends requests straight to your Express `app` object; no port needed. Export `app` separately from the file that calls `listen`.
Assert on **status codes, response bodies and headers**: the contract your frontend depends on.
Use a separate test database (or an in-memory store) and reset it before each test, so tests don't depend on each other.

demo.say: A factory gives every test a fresh app with empty data. In real code, import it from app.js.
beforeEach resets state, so the order of tests doesn't matter.
A real POST through Express. Check the status and the exact body.
The unhappy path: validation must answer 400.
supertest can assert headers too.

practice.task: Add a test that a body over 10kb gets a 413 when the app uses `express.json({ limit: "10kb" })`.
practice.hint: Send `{ title: "x".repeat(20000) }`.

check.q: Why export app separately from app.listen()?
options: So tests can import the app without starting a server
check.why: supertest drives the app object directly.

check.q: Integration tests check…
options: Several parts working together through a real interface
check.why: Here: routing + middleware + handler over HTTP.

advancedLessons.title: End-to-end tests with Playwright
advancedLessons.goal: Test whole user journeys in a real browser.
body: **End-to-end (E2E)** tests drive a real browser through your running app: open the page, click, type, check what's shown. They catch problems unit tests can't, like broken routing, missing env vars and CSS hiding a button.
**Playwright** runs Chromium, Firefox and WebKit, waits for elements automatically, and records traces and videos when tests fail. Set up with `npm init playwright@latest`.
Use the same user-facing locators as Testing Library: `getByRole`, `getByLabel`, `getByText`.
E2E tests are slower and more fragile, so keep them for **critical journeys** (sign up, checkout, the main feature) and use unit tests for the details. That's the **testing pyramid**.

demo.say: Start where a real learner starts, and click the Start button.
Assertions wait automatically until they pass (or time out).
Use the walkthrough like a user would.
Complete the lesson and check the confirmation.
Progress survives navigation: the home page now says Continue.
A phone-sized check that nothing scrolls sideways.

practice.task: Which of these deserve an E2E test? (a) a formatPrice function, (b) the checkout flow, (c) a button's hover color, (d) sign-up then sign-in.
practice.hint: Critical journeys only.

solution.code:
(a) No: a unit test is faster and more precise.
(b) Yes: it's where money is made.
(c) No: visual detail; a screenshot test at most.
(d) Yes: if sign-in breaks, nothing else matters.

check.q: The testing pyramid says to have…
options: Many unit tests, fewer integration tests, few E2E tests
check.why: Fast, precise tests at the base; slow, broad ones at the top.

check.q: Why does Playwright rarely need manual waits?
options: Actions and assertions auto-wait for elements
check.why: Auto-waiting removes most flakiness.

advancedLessons.title: TDD, and running tests in CI
advancedLessons.goal: Write tests first when it helps, and make every push run the tests automatically.
body: **Test-driven development (TDD):** **Red** (write a failing test for the next small behavior), **Green** (write the simplest code that passes), **Refactor** (clean up with the test as a safety net). Repeat.
TDD shines for logic with clear rules: validation, pricing, parsers. It's less useful for exploratory UI work.
**Mock at the boundaries** (network, time, randomness), not your own internal functions. Over-mocking makes tests pass while the real code is broken.
**Continuous integration (CI):** GitHub Actions runs your tests on every push and pull request. A red check means don't merge.

demo.say: Red → green 1: the simplest case. The first version was just lowercase plus replacing spaces.
Red → green 2: punctuation forced the [^a-z0-9]+ rule.
Red → green 3: accents. normalize() splits é into e plus an accent mark, which we then remove.
Red → green 4: trimming. Then refactor, with all four tests protecting you.

practice.task: Write a GitHub Actions workflow that runs `npm ci` and `npm test -- --run` on every push and pull request.
practice.hint: Save it as .github/workflows/test.yml.

solution.code:
name: Tests
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test -- --run

check.q: The TDD cycle is…
check.why: Failing test, passing code, then clean up.

check.q: What should you usually mock?
check.why: Over-mocking hides real bugs.

modules.blurb: The coding tests and questions junior developers get asked most.
intermediate: Build a component live: tabs, accordion, modal
advanced: Trees and graphs: BFS and DFS

lessons.title: How junior coding interviews work
lessons.goal: Know the format and a method for any problem.
body: Junior frontend interviews usually mix: a **take-home** or live **coding problem** (strings, arrays, objects), a **build-a-component** task in React, **concept questions** (HTML, CSS, JS, React), and **talking through your projects**.

Use this method out loud for every problem. **1. Restate** the problem and ask about edge cases (empty input? negative numbers?). **2. Give examples** with input and expected output. **3. Plan** in plain words before coding. **4. Code** the simple version first. **5. Test** with your examples, out loud. **6. Improve**, and talk about speed (Big-O) if asked.
Interviewers grade **communication** as much as the answer. Silence is the most common reason juniors fail.
It's fine to say "I'd look that method up". Then describe what it does.

example.code:
Problem: "Return the most frequent character in a string."

1. Restate: "So for 'banana' I return 'a'? What about a tie, or an empty string?"
2. Examples: 'banana' -> 'a'   'abc' -> 'a' (first wins)   '' -> null
3. Plan: count each char in an object, then find the key with the biggest count.
4. Code it.
5. Test: run 'banana', 'abc' and '' by hand.
6. Improve: "One pass to count plus one pass over the keys, so O(n)."

demo.say: Ask about edge cases before writing any code.
Write examples down. They become your tests.
Plan in plain words. The interviewer can correct you early.
Walk through your own examples out loud.
Finish with how fast it is.

practice.task: Practice the method on 'count the vowels in a string', speaking each step out loud. Time yourself: aim for under 10 minutes.
practice.hint: Edge cases: uppercase letters? empty string? Is 'y' a vowel?

check.q: What should you do first in a coding interview?
options: Restate the problem and ask about edge cases
check.why: Clarifying shows thinking and avoids solving the wrong problem.

project.title: Mock interview
project.brief: Do a 45-minute practice interview: two coding problems from the list (one Easy, one Medium) while explaining out loud, three concept questions, and a 2-minute walkthrough of one of your projects.
steps: Pick problems you haven't seen
Set a timer and talk through the 6-step method
Record yourself, or practice with a friend
Answer three questions from the list without notes
Explain one project: the problem, your choices, what you'd improve
test: Both solutions pass their test cases
You asked at least one clarifying question per problem
You stated the Big-O of each solution

intermediateLessons.title: Patterns: two pointers, sliding window, hash maps
intermediateLessons.goal: Recognize the three patterns behind most junior and mid-level array and string problems.
body: **Hash map** (a JavaScript `Map` or object): when you need "have I seen this?" or "how many of each?", trade memory for speed. It turns O(n²) nested loops into O(n).
**Two pointers**: one index at each end (or a slow and a fast pointer) moving toward each other. Good for sorted arrays, palindromes, and removing items in place.
**Sliding window**: a range `[left, right]` that grows to the right and shrinks from the left. Good for "longest/shortest substring or subarray that…" problems.
Say the pattern out loud in interviews: "This looks like a sliding window because…". It shows how you think.

demo.say: A Map remembers each character's last position. The window starts empty.
Grow the window to the right. On a repeat inside the window, jump left past it.
Record the position and keep the best window length.
Two pointers: read scans everything, write marks where the next non-zero goes.
"abc" is the longest unique run.
Zeros moved to the end, order kept, no extra array.

practice.task: Which pattern fits? (a) Is there a pair in a SORTED array summing to 10? (b) Find the first non-repeating character. (c) The maximum sum of any 3 consecutive numbers.
practice.hint: Sorted + pair → ?, counting → ?, fixed-size range → ?

solution.code:
(a) Two pointers from both ends
(b) Hash map of counts, then a second pass
(c) Sliding window of size 3

check.q: Turning nested loops into one pass usually uses…
check.why: Lookups in a Map are O(1).

check.q: "Longest substring with at most k distinct letters" suggests…
check.why: Grow and shrink a window while tracking counts.

intermediateLessons.title: Recursion and building a component live
intermediateLessons.goal: Solve problems with recursion, and handle a live "build a component" round.
body: A recursive function calls itself on a **smaller** input. It needs a **base case** that stops it: without one, it runs until the stack overflows.
Good fits: nested data (flatten arrays, walk a folder tree or a menu), and splitting problems in half.

Live component rounds (tabs, accordion, modal, autocomplete) are graded on: working state, **keyboard and screen-reader support**, clean structure, and talking through trade-offs. Start simple, get it working, then improve it.
Tell them what you'd add with more time: tests, edge cases, animation, loading states.

demo.say: Base case: a file has no children, so return its size.
Recursive case: the folder's size is the sum of its children's sizes.
One piece of state: which tab is active.
Arrow keys move between tabs, wrapping around at the ends.
ARIA roles and states tell screen readers it's a tab list.
Only the active tab is in the Tab order (a "roving tabindex").
The panel is linked to its tab.

practice.task: Write a recursive `countKeys(obj)` that counts every key in a nested object (including keys inside nested objects).
practice.hint: For each key: 1, plus countKeys(value) if the value is an object.

check.q: What stops recursion?
check.why: Without a base case, it never stops.

check.q: In a live component round, what comes first?
options: A simple working version, then improvements
check.why: Working beats polished-but-unfinished.

intermediateLessons.title: Talking about your projects (STAR)
intermediateLessons.goal: Explain a project and a challenge clearly in two minutes.
body: Use **STAR**: **S**ituation (the context), **T**ask (your goal), **A**ction (what *you* did, and why), **R**esult (the outcome, with a number if you have one).
Pick a real **technical decision**: why server components, why you lifted state, how you fixed a bug. Interviewers dig into the "why".
Be honest about tools, including AI help: "I used Claude to scaffold the layout, then wrote the auth flow and tests myself" is a strong answer when you can walk through the code.
End with what you'd improve. It shows you can judge your own work.

example.code:
S  "In my internship project, Summarist, users saw the logged-out page flash
    for a second after refreshing, even when they were signed in."
T  "I needed the app to wait for Firebase to restore the session."
A  "I added an AuthListener that writes the user to Redux, with an
    'initializing' flag. Protected pages show a skeleton until it's false,
    and a separate isPremium value starts as null meaning 'still checking'."
R  "The flash is gone, and premium users are never wrongly redirected
    to the plans page."
+  "Next I'd move the premium check to the server so it can't be bypassed."

demo.say: Situation: a specific, visible problem.
Task: what you set out to do.
Action: what you built, using the right terms.
Result: what changed for users.
Bonus: what you'd do next, which shows judgment.

practice.task: Write a STAR answer for one bug you fixed in any of your projects. Keep it under 120 words, and say it out loud in under 90 seconds.
practice.hint: Choose a bug where you learned why it happened, not just how to fix it.

solution.code:
There's no single answer. Check yours against this list:
- Does Situation name the project and the symptom?
- Is Action about what YOU did, with the reason?
- Is Result specific?
- Could you answer "why did that happen?" if they asked?

check.q: STAR stands for…
check.why: Situation, Task, Action, Result.

advancedLessons.title: Big-O: how code scales
advancedLessons.goal: Estimate how running time grows with input size, and explain it in an interview.
body: **Big-O** describes how work grows as input grows, ignoring constants. O(1) constant, O(log n) halving (binary search), O(n) one pass, O(n log n) good sorting, O(n²) nested loops over the same data.

Count the **loops over the input**: one loop is O(n), a loop inside a loop over the same array is O(n²). Array methods are loops too: `includes`, `indexOf` and `find` are O(n), so calling them inside a loop is O(n²).
**Space complexity** counts extra memory: a Map of n items is O(n) space.
In interviews, state it plainly: "This is O(n) time and O(n) space because of the Map. The brute force was O(n²)."

demo.say: Compare every pair: a loop inside a loop is O(n²).
One pass with a Set: O(n) time, O(n) extra space.
For 10 items the difference is small.
100× more input means about 10,000× more work for O(n²), but only 100× for O(n).
Same answers; only the scaling differs.

advancedLessons.title: Trees and graphs: BFS and DFS
advancedLessons.goal: Traverse trees and graphs, and know which search finds the shortest path.
body: A **graph** is nodes plus connections (edges). A **tree** is a graph with no cycles and one root, like the DOM, a folder structure or comment threads.
**DFS (depth-first)** goes as deep as possible before backing up. Use recursion or a stack. Good for exploring everything, like counting files or finding connected regions.
**BFS (breadth-first)** explores level by level with a **queue**. In an unweighted graph, **BFS finds the shortest path**.
Always track **visited** nodes in graphs, or cycles will loop forever.

demo.say: Pages and their links, as an adjacency list. checkout links back to home, so there's a cycle.
BFS: a queue of paths, and a visited set so the cycle can't loop forever.
Take the oldest path first. That's what makes it level by level.
Queue each unvisited neighbor as a longer path.
DFS by recursion: count every page reachable from here.
BFS found the shortest route, skipping the longer one through product.
There's no path from team.
All 7 pages are reachable from home.

advancedLessons.title: Frontend system design and the offer stage
advancedLessons.goal: Structure a frontend design interview, and handle behavioral and salary questions.
body: **Frontend system design** questions: "Design a news feed", "Design an autocomplete", "Design a photo gallery". You have about 45 minutes and no single right answer.

Use a framework: **Requirements** (features, users, devices; ask questions) → **Architecture** (components, data flow, server vs client) → **Data model and API** (endpoints, pagination, caching) → **Deep dive** (performance, accessibility, loading/error states, offline) → **Trade-offs**.

**Behavioral** questions ("Tell me about a conflict", "a time you failed") use STAR. Prepare 5–6 stories you can adapt. A career change is a strength: you've learned new domains before and you bring real-world experience.

**Salary:** research the range first (levels.fyi, Glassdoor, local job posts). When asked early, give a researched range or ask for theirs. Negotiate the whole offer: base, sign-on, PTO, remote days, learning budget. Get it in writing.

example.code:
DESIGN AN AUTOCOMPLETE (search box with suggestions)

1 Requirements
  - Suggestions after 2+ characters, max 8, keyboard selectable
  - Fast on slow phones; accessible to screen readers

2 Architecture
  <SearchBox> → useDebouncedValue(query, 250) → useSuggestions(q)
  <SuggestionList> as role="listbox", options as role="option"

3 Data / API
  GET /api/suggest?q=rea → [{ id, label }]
  Cache by query (in memory, LRU of 50); cancel stale requests (AbortController)

4 Deep dive
  - Keyboard: ↑ ↓ to move, Enter to pick, Esc to close (aria-activedescendant)
  - Announce "8 suggestions" in a live region
  - Highlight the matched part; handle empty, error and slow states

5 Trade-offs
  - Debounce delay vs. responsiveness
  - Client-side filtering of a small static list vs. server search for large data

demo.say: Start with requirements, out loud. Ask; don't assume.
Name the components and how data flows between them.
The API shape, caching and cancelling. This is where seniority shows.
Accessibility and edge states are what most candidates forget.
End with trade-offs: there's no perfect design, only choices.

practice.task: Outline "Design an infinite-scroll photo feed" using the five steps. Spend 10 minutes, then compare with the checklist in the solution.
practice.hint: Think about pagination, image loading, memory and accessibility.

solution.code:
Checklist:
- Cursor-based pagination (not page numbers) so new posts don't cause duplicates
- IntersectionObserver on a sentinel to load the next page
- Responsive images (srcset), lazy-loading, reserved aspect-ratio boxes (no layout shift)
- Virtualize the list after a few hundred items to save memory
- Loading skeletons, error + retry, and an end-of-feed message
- A "Load more" button as an accessible alternative to endless scroll
- Keep the scroll position when returning from a photo's detail page
