problems.title: Reverse a string
problems.prompt: Write `reverse(str)` that returns the string backwards.
problems.approach: Split into characters, reverse the array, join it back. Or loop from the end.
problems.followUp: Why [...str] instead of str.split('')? Spread handles emoji correctly.

problems.title: Palindrome check
problems.prompt: Write `isPalindrome(str)` that ignores case and anything that isn't a letter or number.
problems.approach: Clean the string with a regex, lowercase it, then compare it to its reverse. Two pointers from both ends is the O(1)-space version.
tests: A man, a plan, a canal: Panama
problems.followUp: Solve it with two pointers and no extra string.

problems.title: FizzBuzz
problems.prompt: Return an array from 1 to n: 'Fizz' for multiples of 3, 'Buzz' for 5, 'FizzBuzz' for both, otherwise the number.
problems.approach: Check 15 (both) first, then 3, then 5.
problems.followUp: Why does the 15 check have to come first?

problems.title: Largest number without Math.max
problems.prompt: Write `largest(nums)` that returns the biggest number, or null for an empty array.
problems.approach: Keep the best value so far, starting from the first item, and compare each number.
problems.followUp: Why start at nums[0] and not 0? (Try it with all negative numbers.)

problems.title: Remove duplicates
problems.prompt: Write `unique(arr)` returning the items with duplicates removed, keeping first-seen order.
problems.approach: A Set only keeps unique values and remembers insertion order.
problems.followUp: Do it without a Set, using an object to track what you've seen.

problems.title: Anagram check
problems.prompt: Write `isAnagram(a, b)`: true if b uses exactly the same letters as a (ignore spaces and case).
problems.approach: Normalize both strings, then compare sorted letters, or count letters in an object.
problems.followUp: Sorting is O(n log n). Make it O(n) with a counting object.

problems.title: Two Sum
problems.prompt: Given an array of numbers and a target, return the indexes of the two numbers that add up to the target, or null if there are none.
problems.approach: Brute force checks every pair: O(n²). Better: one pass with a Map from number to index, checking whether target − n has already been seen: O(n).
problems.followUp: Explain why the Map version is O(n).

problems.title: Most frequent character
problems.prompt: Return the character that appears most often. On a tie, return the one that appears first. Return null for an empty string.
problems.approach: Count with an object or Map, then find the highest count. A Map keeps first-seen order, so ties go to the earliest character.
problems.followUp: What changes if you need to ignore spaces?

problems.title: Flatten a nested array
problems.prompt: Write `flatten(arr)` that turns [1, [2, [3, [4]]]] into [1, 2, 3, 4] without using .flat().
problems.approach: Loop over the items: if an item is an array, flatten it (recursion) and spread the result in; otherwise push it.
problems.followUp: Add a depth parameter like .flat(depth).

problems.title: Capitalize each word
problems.prompt: Write `titleCase(str)` so 'the quick fox' becomes 'The Quick Fox'.
problems.approach: Split on spaces, uppercase the first letter of each word, join back together.
problems.followUp: What happens with double spaces? Does your version keep them?

problems.title: Longest substring without repeats
problems.prompt: Return the length of the longest part of the string with no repeated characters.
problems.approach: Keep a window [left, right] and a Map of each character's last index. When a character repeats inside the window, move left past its previous position.
problems.followUp: What's the time complexity, and why isn't it O(n²)?

problems.title: Valid brackets
problems.prompt: Return true if every (, [ and { in the string is closed by the matching bracket in the right order.
problems.approach: Push opening brackets onto a stack. For a closing bracket, the top of the stack must be its partner. At the end the stack must be empty.
problems.followUp: Where would you use this in a real app? (Think: code editors, form input for formulas.)

problems.title: Group anagrams
problems.prompt: Group words that are anagrams of each other. Return the groups in the order their first word appears.
problems.approach: Sort each word's letters to make a key, and collect words under that key in a Map (which keeps insertion order).
problems.followUp: Can you build the key without sorting? (A 26-letter count string.)

problems.title: Move zeros to the end
problems.prompt: Move every 0 to the end of the array, keeping the order of the other numbers. Change the array in place and return it.
problems.approach: A write pointer marks where the next non-zero goes. Swap each non-zero into it.
problems.followUp: Why is in-place important? What does it save?

problems.title: Chunk an array
problems.prompt: Split an array into groups of `size`. The last group may be smaller.
problems.approach: Step through the array `size` at a time and slice.
problems.followUp: Where does this show up in UI work? (Pagination, rows of cards.)

problems.title: Binary search
problems.prompt: Given a SORTED array and a target, return the target's index, or -1. It must be faster than checking every item.
problems.approach: Look at the middle. If it's too small, search the right half; if it's too big, the left half. Halving each step gives O(log n).
problems.followUp: How many steps does it take for 1,000,000 items? (About 20.)

problems.title: Merge overlapping intervals
problems.prompt: Given [start, end] pairs, merge every overlapping pair and return the result sorted by start. Touching intervals like [1,3] and [3,5] count as overlapping.
problems.approach: Sort by start. Walk through, extending the last merged interval when the next one starts before (or at) its end; otherwise push a new one. O(n log n) for the sort.
problems.followUp: Where would this appear in a real app? (Calendar availability, booking systems.)

problems.title: Top k frequent words
problems.prompt: Return the k most frequent words, most frequent first. Break ties alphabetically.
problems.approach: Count with a Map, then sort the entries by count descending, then by word ascending, and take k.
problems.followUp: With millions of words and small k, how could a heap beat sorting everything?

problems.title: Shortest path in a grid
problems.prompt: In a grid of 0s (open) and 1s (walls), return the fewest steps from the top-left to the bottom-right moving up, down, left or right, or -1 if impossible.
problems.approach: BFS from [0,0] with a queue of [row, col, steps] and a visited set. The first time you reach the goal is the shortest path.
problems.followUp: Why is the queue read with an index instead of shift()? (shift is O(n).)

problems.title: LRU cache
problems.prompt: Simulate an LRU cache with a capacity. `lru(capacity, ops)` gets ops like ["put", key, value] and ["get", key], and returns the results of every get (-1 when missing). When full, evict the least recently used key.
problems.approach: A JavaScript Map remembers insertion order. On get, delete and re-insert the key to mark it as recently used. On put when full, evict the first key (map.keys().next().value). Every operation is O(1).
problems.followUp: Without a Map's ordering, you'd use a hash map plus a doubly linked list. Explain why.

problems.title: Count islands
problems.prompt: In a grid of 1s (land) and 0s (water), count the islands. Land cells connect up, down, left and right.
problems.approach: Scan every cell. When you find unvisited land, count an island and flood-fill it with DFS (marking cells as visited) so it isn't counted again.
problems.followUp: Why copy the grid first? (Don't mutate the caller's input.)

questions.a: === compares value and type with no conversion. == converts types first, so "5" == 5 is true. Use === by default.
const can't be reassigned; let can. Both are block-scoped. var is function-scoped and hoisted, which causes bugs, so avoid it.
Every element is content + padding + border + margin. box-sizing: border-box makes width include padding and border.
Tags like <nav>, <main> and <button> carry meaning for screen readers, search engines and other developers, and they come with built-in behavior like keyboard support.
It lets you write asynchronous Promise code that reads top to bottom. await pauses the async function until the Promise settles.
Props are inputs passed from a parent and are read-only. State is data a component owns and changes with its setter, which triggers a re-render.

questions.q: Why do list items need a key in React?
questions.a: Keys tell React which item is which between renders, so it updates the right DOM nodes. Use stable unique ids, not indexes, when lists change.
An API that uses HTTP methods on resource URLs: GET /books reads, POST /books creates, PUT/PATCH updates, DELETE removes, with status codes and usually JSON.
The browser's in-memory tree of the page's elements. JavaScript reads and changes it, and the browser re-draws.

questions.q: Server vs client components in Next.js?
questions.a: Server components render on the server, can fetch data directly and ship no JS. Client components ("use client") run in the browser and can use state, effects and events.

questions.q: What is SQL injection and how do you prevent it?
questions.a: Inserting user input directly into a SQL string lets attackers run their own SQL. Use parameterized queries (placeholders like $1) instead.
A function that runs between the request and your route: (req, res, next). It's used for logging (morgan), parsing bodies, auth and more. Order matters.
